details: {"chapter_heading":"1. Mental Performance Curriculum","groups":[{"blocks":[{"text":"1.2.1 Why this matters most in boxing","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Excessive arousal produces muscular tension. Tension destroys punch speed (co-contraction of antagonists slows the limb), accuracy (fine motor control degrades), and endurance (tense muscles consume oxygen doing nothing) — simultaneously. This is why the single most common diagnosis for a beginner “gassing out in round one” is not poor conditioning but tension.","type":"text"},{"text":"There is also a mechanical dimension: a tense arm has less effective mass transfer than a relaxed arm that stiffens at impact. The technical ideal is relaxed between actions, rigid at impact — which is an arousal-regulation skill as much as a technical one.","type":"text"},{"text":"1.2.2 The protocol","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Diaphragmatic breathing — daily, 5–10 min - Sit or lie with one hand on the belly, one on the chest. The belly hand moves; the chest hand does not - Progress to a 4-2-6 pattern: inhale 4 s, hold 2 s, exhale 6 s. The extended exhale is the parasympathetic driver - Then practise it in the 60-second interval between rounds, on the bag and in sparring, until it is automatic. This is the transfer step everyone omits - Morning and pre-sleep","type":"text"},{"text":"Progressive muscular relaxation — 2×/week, 15–20 min - Full-body protocol: tense each muscle group 5 s, release 15 s, moving systematically - Then build an abbreviated version usable in the ring: jaw, shoulders, hands — three checkpoints you can run in two seconds between exchanges","type":"text"},{"text":"Cue words for relaxation - Anchor 2–3 words during training (“loose,” “breathe,” “long,” “soft hands”) and deploy them in competition - The anchoring matters: the word must be paired with the physical state hundreds of times in training before it will produce the state under pressure","type":"text"},{"text":"HRV biofeedback — 3–5×/week, 10–15 min, if available - Resonance-frequency breathing training with a validated app and a chest strap - The evidence is moderate and the practice is harmless; worth doing if you will do it consistently","type":"text"},{"text":"1.2.3 The boxing-specific application","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Explosive-loose alternation drill. On the bag: 3 × 3 min alternating 5 s of explosive output with 10 s of completely loose movement. The loose phase is the trained skill — most boxers cannot actually go loose on command, and it shows in round 3.","type":"text"},{"text":"Breathing rhythm coupled to punching. Short sharp exhale with each punch; full breath in the gaps. Boxers who hold their breath during exchanges are the ones whose arms fill up.","type":"text"},{"text":"Jaw and shoulder audit. Every round, once: check the jaw is not clenched (beyond biting the mouthguard) and the shoulders are not at the ears.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[{"drill_id":"drl_03b9c6da4f9fe9","name":"Diaphragmatic breathing"},{"drill_id":"drl_44173cce2543ae","name":"Progressive muscular relaxation"},{"drill_id":"drl_46040657d32624","name":"Cue words for relaxation"},{"drill_id":"drl_2b27785918f43a","name":"HRV biofeedback"},{"drill_id":"drl_6a9ec801add8ab","name":"Explosive-loose alternation drill"},{"drill_id":"drl_43d923174a2e13","name":"Breathing rhythm coupled to punching"},{"drill_id":"drl_f5d10bfec46b61","name":"Jaw and shoulder audit"}],"heading":"1.2 Skill A — Arousal regulation","order":1,"section":"LR-146","source":"LR-146 (The Long Road, Part 7, 1.2 Skill A — Arousal regulation)","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"1.3.1 The four attentional states","type":"subheading"},{"text":"In a bout, attention must shift between:","type":"text"},{"header":["State","Content","When"],"rows":[{"Content":"Ring position, opponent’s whole body, corner, clock","State":"Broad-external","When":"Between exchanges, resetting"},{"Content":"A specific target, a specific tell","State":"Narrow-external","When":"Entering an exchange"},{"Content":"A single technical or tactical cue","State":"Narrow-internal","When":"Corner instruction, resetting after a mistake"},{"Content":"Rumination, self-evaluation, catastrophizing (“I’m losing,” “he’s too strong”)","State":"Broad-internal","When":"Never useful in a bout. This is the failure state"}],"type":"table"},{"text":"The skill is not “concentrate harder.” It is shifting deliberately between the first three and noticing when you have slipped into the fourth.","type":"text"},{"text":"1.3.2 The protocol","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Mindfulness practice — daily, 10 min - Any well-structured protocol. The mechanism is training the noticing and returning of attention, which is precisely the skill required when your mind drifts to the scorecard in round 2 - Mindfulness carries one of the better effect sizes in the sport psychology literature (~1.35 in a meta-analytical review of athletic populations)","type":"text"},{"text":"Attentional shifting drill - During bag work, the coach calls “wide” (scan the whole room while continuing to work) or “narrow” (single target only) at random intervals. 3 × 2 min","type":"text"},{"text":"Distraction training - Perform technical work with deliberate noise, movement, and disruption present. Music at volume, people moving nearby, someone talking to you. Progressively increase","type":"text"},{"text":"The refocusing routine — the highest-value item in this section - A three-step reset: physical cue → breath → task cue. Example: touch gloves together → one exhale → “jab first” - Rehearse it until it takes under 2 seconds - Deploy it after every mistake in training, without exception, so it is automatic in competition. Most boxers have no trained response to making a mistake, which is why one clean shot taken can cost them a round","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[{"drill_id":"drl_9eef0052f5db82","name":"Mindfulness practice"},{"drill_id":"drl_608fcef4de2779","name":"Attentional shifting drill"},{"drill_id":"drl_95af631decae78","name":"Distraction training"},{"drill_id":"drl_6219fca7255c06","name":"The refocusing routine"}],"heading":"1.3 Skill B — Attentional control","order":2,"section":"LR-147","source":"LR-147 (The Long Road, Part 7, 1.3 Skill B — Attentional control)","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"1.4.1 The PETTLEP framework","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Imagery works better when it resembles the real thing along seven dimensions:","type":"text"},{"header":["Element","Application"],"rows":[{"Application":"In kit, standing, gloves on where practical — not lying in bed","Element":"Physical"},{"Application":"The actual venue if known; the actual gym otherwise. Look at photos of the venue","Element":"Environment"},{"Application":"The specific task at your current skill level, not a fantasy version","Element":"Task"},{"Application":"Real time. Not slow motion. A round takes three minutes to image properly","Element":"Timing"},{"Application":"Update the content as skill develops","Element":"Learning"},{"Application":"Include the nerves. Practice Design: How to Actually Teach This","groups":[{"blocks":[{"text":"Every skill climbs this ladder, and a boxer sits at different rungs for different skills simultaneously.","type":"text"},{"header":["Rung","Format","Develops","Head-impact cost","Typical share of skill time"],"rows":[{"Develops":"Pattern formation, self-perception, high volume at zero cost","Format":"Shadow / mirror","Head-impact cost":"Zero","Rung":"1","Typical share of skill time":"10–15%"},{"Develops":"Mechanics with feedback","Format":"Air work with external cues + video","Head-impact cost":"Zero","Rung":"2","Typical share of skill time":"5–10%"},{"Develops":"Force production, rhythm, conditioning","Format":"Bag / pads, predictable feed","Head-impact cost":"Zero","Rung":"3","Typical share of skill time":"20–25%"},{"Develops":"Perception-action coupling begins","Format":"Pads with unpredictable feed","Head-impact cost":"Zero","Rung":"4","Typical share of skill time":"10–15%"},{"Develops":"Live information, safely","Format":"Cooperative partner, low speed, defined roles","Head-impact cost":"Near zero","Rung":"5","Typical share of skill time":"15–20%"},{"Develops":"Skill emerging under real pressure","Format":"Constrained live (one hand, touch only, body only, defense only)","Head-impact cost":"Low","Rung":"6","Typical share of skill time":"20–25%"},{"Develops":"Integration","Format":"Open live at controlled intensity","Head-impact cost":"Moderate","Rung":"7","Typical share of skill time":"5–10%"},{"Develops":"Expression under full demand","Format":"Competition-representative","Head-impact cost":"High","Rung":"8","Typical share of skill time":"2–5%"}],"type":"table"},{"text":"The central claim of this section: rungs 5 and 6 do most of the learning at a fraction of rungs 7 and 8’s cost. Gyms that jump from rung 3 to rung 8 — pads straight to hard sparring — buy their skill development with brain trauma and produce worse boxers than gyms that live in rungs 4–6.","type":"text"},{"text":"Note the suggested time shares. Most gyms spend far more than 25% on rung 3 (bag work) and far less than 20% on rung 6. Reallocating that is free improvement.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"2.1 The coupling ladder","order":1,"section":"LR-113","source":"LR-113 (The Long Road, Part 6, 2.1 The coupling ladder)","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"Constraints are the primary coaching tool. improves performance during practice and degrades retention. The fix is not necessarily less total load; it is variability — genuinely easy days that are actually easy, and hard days that are genuinely hard.","type":"text"},{"text":"On the acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR): you will encounter this metric. It is intuitive and widely used, and it has been substantively criticized on methodological grounds — the mathematical coupling of numerator and denominator, arbitrary time windows, and questions about whether it predicts anything beyond simple weekly load change. Conditioning: Energy System Development","groups":[{"blocks":[{"text":"3.2.1 The protocol","type":"subheading"},{"text":"30 seconds maximal effort, 3–4 minutes recovery, 4–6 repetitions. Total work: 2–3 minutes","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Intent is the entire point. No pacing strategy. Attack from the first second and accept the decline","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Modality: curved treadmill is ideal (genuine maximal output with measurable speed); air bike or Watt bike is an excellent low-impact alternative; outdoor sprints on grass or track work with distance targets","type":"bullet"},{"text":"3.2.2 The mechanism, explained properly","type":"subheading"},{"text":"This is where most people’s understanding is wrong. Thirty-second all-out sprints look purely anaerobic. They are one of the most potent aerobic stimuli available, and the reason is molecular.","type":"text"},{"text":"Maximal 30-second efforts rapidly deplete phosphocreatine and glycogen and generate substantial metabolic disturbance — a rising AMP:ATP ratio, calcium flux, and reactive oxygen species. These perturbations activate signalling kinases, principally AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) and p38 MAPK. These converge on PGC-1α, the master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis, driving it into the nucleus where it upregulates the expression of mitochondrial genes.","type":"text"},{"text":"The direct human evidence is specific: an acute bout of 4 × 30 s all-out cycling activated p38 MAPK and AMPK in the cytosol, and nuclear PGC-1α protein increased 3 hours into recovery, coinciding with increased mRNA expression of mitochondrial genes (Little et al., 2011). Comparative work found that sprint-interval exercise, but not duration-matched moderate continuous exercise, increased PGC-1α protein content and p53 phosphorylation in nuclear fractions of human skeletal muscle — suggesting SIT is a time-efficient and possibly superior stimulus for these early molecular events (Bartlett and colleagues; see also Granata et al.).","type":"text"},{"text":"So: two minutes of total work, done properly, is a genuine mitochondrial stimulus. That is the justification for a protocol that looks absurdly brief for a sport as demanding as boxing.","type":"text"},{"text":"Secondary benefits: - Recruits high-threshold motor units similarly to heavy resistance training, with potential benefit to force production and RFD - Trains carbohydrate utilization at high rates — relevant because boxing’s high-force actions are carbohydrate-fuelled - Produces extreme acidosis, which is both a physiological stimulus and a psychological one","type":"text"},{"text":"A caution worth knowing: repeated identical HIIT stimuli appear to blunt the molecular response over time — one study of 40 HIIT sessions found reduced exercise-induced increases in nuclear PGC-1α and p53. This is a mechanistic argument for progressive overload and for varying the stimulus rather than repeating the same session for months.","type":"text"},{"text":"3.2.3 Monitoring and progression","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Record speed or power at 7 s, 17 s and 27 s of each repetition. This gives peak output and rate of drop-off, which is far more informative than a single average","type":"bullet"},{"text":"On a curved treadmill or Watt bike this is straightforward. Outdoors, set distance targets and compute speed","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Progression: 4 reps → 6 reps over 4–6 weeks → reduce recovery to 2.5–3 min → then progress by output at fixed volume","type":"bullet"},{"text":"3.2.4 Placement and cautions","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Early in preparation blocks, far from heavy sparring weeks and competition","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Once weekly is sufficient","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Positioned away from sparring in both directions","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Use caution with: heavier boxers, boxers returning from injury, and anyone unaccustomed to high-speed running. Build in gradually or use the bike. A 90 kg boxer doing all-out treadmill sprints in week one of training is an injury waiting to happen","type":"bullet"}],"drill_refs":[{"drill_id":"drl_dbe3f9dd2d62cc","name":"Sprint Interval Training (SIT)"}],"heading":"3.2 Method A — Sprint Interval Training (SIT): peripheral adaptation","order":1,"section":"LR-099","source":"LR-099 (The Long Road, Part 5, 3.2 Method A — Sprint Interval Training (SIT): peripheral adaptation)","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"3.3.1 The protocols","type":"subheading"},{"header":["Protocol","Structure","Repetitions"],"rows":[{"Protocol":"4:2","Repetitions":"3–5","Structure":"4 min work : 2 min recovery"},{"Protocol":"6:3","Repetitions":"3","Structure":"6 min work : 3 min recovery"},{"Protocol":"8:4","Repetitions":"2–3","Structure":"8 min work : 4 min recovery"}],"type":"table"},{"text":"3.3.2 The actual prescription variable: time above 90% HRmax","type":"subheading"},{"text":"The protocol is a vehicle. The target is 6–12 minutes accumulated at or above 90% of maximum heart rate — the “red zone.” That is the prescription. If a 4:2 × 4 session only puts you above 90% for four minutes, the session failed regardless of how hard it felt.","type":"text"},{"text":"The mechanism: sustained stress on cardiac output forces the heart to operate near maximal pumping capacity, driving central adaptations — increased stroke volume, left-ventricular compliance, plasma and blood volume. These are the determinants of oxygen delivery, complementary to SIT’s effect on oxygen utilization.","type":"text"},{"text":"The specificity justification: heart rate data from sparring and competition show boxers operating in exactly this zone — above 93% HRmax in rounds 1–2, above 97% in round 3. So although running intervals do not look like boxing, they impose the same physiological demand. This is the correct answer to “but it isn’t boxing-specific.”","type":"text"},{"text":"3.3.3 Manipulations to increase red-zone time","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Break the interval into short repeats: a 4-minute interval as 8 × (20 s hard / 10 s float) allows higher running speeds and often more red-zone time than 4 continuous minutes","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Pyramid structures: 1-2-3-4-3-2-1 minutes with proportional recoveries, challenging the athlete across a range of intensities","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Start the interval faster to reach the red zone sooner, then hold","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Reduce recovery slightly so heart rate does not fall as far between intervals","type":"bullet"},{"text":"3.3.4 Prescription from test data","type":"subheading"},{"text":"If you have 30-15 IFT data, prescribe as percentages of VIFT: - 4-minute intervals: 85–90% VIFT - 15 s / 15 s repeats: 95–105% VIFT - 30 s / 30 s repeats: 90–100% VIFT","type":"text"},{"text":"This is far more precise than “hard” and it lets you progress by re-testing VIFT rather than by feel.","type":"text"},{"text":"3.3.5 Placement","type":"subheading"},{"text":"1–2×/week, year-round. This is the workhorse method — the one that stays in the program in every phase.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[{"drill_id":"drl_3cc110cc6213ba","name":"High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT)"}],"heading":"3.3 Method B — High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT): central adaptation","order":2,"section":"LR-100","source":"LR-100 (The Long Road, Part 5, 3.3 Method B — High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT): central adaptation)","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"3.4.1 The protocol","type":"subheading"},{"text":"2 minutes high-intensity effort, 3 minutes recovery, 6–8 repetitions","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Target physiological response: 12–14 mmol·L⁻¹ blood lactate — at or above competitive bout values","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Measure lactate if you can; if not, use the subjective marker (significant burning, heavy breathing, all intervals completed with the last 30 seconds genuinely hard) and the objective marker (output per interval)","type":"bullet"},{"text":"3.4.2 The mechanism","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Repeated high-intensity efforts generate high glycolytic flux and consequent hydrogen ion accumulation. H⁺ is the actual problem — it interferes with contractile function and with glycolytic enzymes, and it stimulates nerve endings producing the burning sensation and driving perceived exertion.","type":"text"},{"text":"Repeated exposure upregulates buffering systems: intracellular buffers (carnosine, phosphates, bicarbonate), monocarboxylate transporters that shuttle lactate and H⁺ out of the muscle, and the capacity to clear and oxidize lactate. These function, in effect, as mops.","type":"text"},{"text":"Why it matters tactically: stoppages and knockouts are typically preceded by sequences of high-force actions. The boxer who can produce such a sequence, recover, and produce another has a weapon. The boxer who produces one and then needs ninety seconds does not.","type":"text"},{"text":"3.4.3 Placement, progression, and cautions","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Specific preparation phase, 2–3×/week during a dedicated 3–4 week block. Reduce to 1×/week for maintenance","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Progression: 6 → 8 reps → increase intensity at fixed volume → reduce recovery","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Highly fatiguing. Do not stack with hard sparring in the same 24 hours in either direction — both produce heavy acidosis and central fatigue","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Stop the session if output falls more than 15% below the first interval. Past that point you are training fatigue tolerance, not buffering","type":"bullet"},{"text":"3.4.4 The supplement adjunct","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Two of the IOC-recognized supplements act directly on this quality: - Sodium bicarbonate raises extracellular buffering capacity acutely (0.2–0.3 g/kg, 60–150 min pre-event). GI distress is common and must be trialled extensively - β-alanine raises intramuscular carnosine over weeks of loading (3.2–6.4 g/day in divided doses for 4+ weeks)","type":"text"},{"text":"Neither replaces the training. Both are legitimate adjuncts. Details in Part 7 §2.6.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[{"drill_id":"drl_0bb18ed31c1b10","name":"Muscle buffering / lactate tolerance"}],"heading":"3.4 Method C — Muscle buffering / lactate tolerance","order":3,"section":"LR-101","source":"LR-101 (The Long Road, Part 5, 3.4 Method C — Muscle buffering / lactate tolerance)","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"3.5.1 The protocol","type":"subheading"},{"text":"30–60 min continuous at 60–75% HRmax, or 2 × 20 min at threshold","type":"bullet"},{"text":"3.5.2 What it is actually for, by phase","type":"subheading"},{"header":["Phase","Purpose"],"rows":[{"Phase":"Phase 1","Purpose":"Genuine aerobic base development. In an untrained person, continuous work at moderate intensity produces real central and peripheral adaptation, and it builds the tissue tolerance required for later high-intensity work"},{"Phase":"Phase 2–4","Purpose":"Tissue conditioning, capillarization, recovery facilitation, active recovery, psychological discipline, and the weight-management contribution of additional energy expenditure"}],"type":"table"},{"text":"3.5.3 Roadwork — its real place","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Roadwork carries enormous cultural weight in boxing and it deserves a fair assessment.","type":"text"},{"text":"What it does well: builds tissue tolerance in the lower limb, provides genuine aerobic stimulus to untrained athletes, offers a low-cost daily habit that develops discipline, allows thinking time and mental rehearsal, and contributes to energy expenditure.","type":"text"},{"text":"What it does poorly: raising the aerobic ceiling in an already-trained athlete, per unit of time. Sixty minutes of steady running is a poor exchange for the same physiological gain available from twenty minutes of properly executed intervals.","type":"text"},{"text":"What it costs: the concurrent-training evidence indicates running produces greater interference with strength adaptation than cycling — likely via eccentric loading and muscle damage — and interference scales with weekly aerobic volume. High-volume road running during a maximal strength block is directly counterproductive.","type":"text"},{"text":"The verdict: retain 1–2 sessions weekly for tissue tolerance, recovery, and the mental component. Stop treating five-mile morning runs as the core of boxing conditioning. During maximal strength and power blocks, shift base work to bike, rower, or swim.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[{"coach_note":"Protocol: 30–60 min continuous at 60–75% HRmax, or 2 × 20 min at threshold","decided":"same drill (Jason 2026-11-02 (D-OQ104); D-PK20 via D-PK55): the Long Road line is a coach note on the link, no new drill","drill_id":"drl_81b9474a9fc367","linked":"repo seed 'Continuous Aerobic Base'","name":"Aerobic base and recovery work"}],"heading":"3.5 Method D — Aerobic base and recovery work","order":4,"section":"LR-102","source":"LR-102 (The Long Road, Part 5, 3.5 Method D — Aerobic base and recovery work)","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"The methods above build capacity. Nutrition, Body Composition and Supplementation","groups":[{"blocks":[{"text":"Before macronutrients, before timing, before supplements: are you eating enough?","type":"text"},{"text":"Chronic low energy availability produces the syndrome described in the IOC’s 2023 consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs), affecting metabolic rate, bone health, immune function, endocrine function, protein synthesis, cardiovascular function, and mental health — in athletes of any sex, in any sport, at any competitive level. Weight-category athletes are among the highest-risk groups. The 2023 statement specifically highlighted new evidence on the role of inadequate carbohydrate intake and the overlap between REDs and overtraining syndrome.","type":"text"},{"text":"The honest scientific position: the REDs model has been substantively challenged. Critics note that energy availability is very difficult to measure accurately in the field, that diagnosis therefore rests largely on generic symptoms, that the symptoms have many possible causes (poor mental health, disordered eating, poor sleep, infection, injury, undiagnosed conditions), and that the model attributes multifactorial problems to a single cause (Areta et al., 2024). That critique is reasonable.","type":"text"},{"text":"It does not change the practical guidance: - Do not train hard in a chronic energy deficit - Treat unexplained fatigue, repeated illness, recurrent injury, mood change, loss of libido, poor sleep, or menstrual disturbance as red flags requiring professional evaluation - If body mass is falling unintentionally by more than ~1% per week, something is wrong","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"2.1 Energy availability first — everything else is secondary","order":1,"section":"LR-154","source":"LR-154 (The Long Road, Part 7, 2.1 Energy availability first — everything else is secondary)","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"Monitor first-morning urine colour (pale straw = adequate) and body mass (same conditions daily)","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Replace 125–150% of session fluid losses when a subsequent session follows","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Sodium matters. Boxers train hot, in long sleeves, and sweat heavily. Plain water in large volumes without sodium can cause problems","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Practical: weigh before and after a hard session; each kilogram lost ≈ 1 litre of fluid. Replace with 1.25–1.5 litres containing sodium","type":"bullet"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"2.4 Hydration","order":2,"section":"LR-157","source":"LR-157 (The Long Road, Part 7, 2.4 Hydration)","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"The IOC consensus statement on dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete (Maughan et al., 2018) identified a short list with adequate evidence for performance benefit: caffeine, creatine monohydrate, nitrate, sodium bicarbonate, and possibly β-alanine. It also emphasized that performance supplements should be considered only where a strong evidence base supports them as safe, legal and effective, ideally after adequacy of dietary practice is ensured, and that they should be trialled thoroughly in training that mimics competition before use in competition.","type":"text"},{"header":["Supplement","Evidence","Boxing relevance","Dosing","Practical notes"],"rows":[{"Boxing relevance":"High — repeated high-intensity efforts, strength and power development, possible cognitive interest","Dosing":"3–5 g/day continuously; optional 20 g/day loading × 5–7 days","Evidence":"Strong","Practical notes":"Causes ~1–2 kg water-weight gain. Start it in the off-season, not in camp. Monohydrate only — the exotic forms have no advantage","Supplement":"Creatine monohydrate"},{"Boxing relevance":"High — reduces perceived exertion, improves alertness, reaction time and power output","Dosing":"3–6 mg/kg, 45–60 min pre-competition","Evidence":"Strong","Practical notes":"Trial in training first. Beware sleep disruption and over-arousal in an already anxious athlete. Habitual high intake blunts the acute effect","Supplement":"Caffeine"},{"Boxing relevance":"Moderate-high — extracellular buffering for exactly the acidosis boxing produces","Dosing":"0.2–0.3 g/kg, 60–150 min pre-event, or split-dose protocols","Evidence":"Good, with high individual variability","Practical notes":"GI distress is common and can ruin a performance. Must be trialled extensively. Split doses and enteric-coated forms reduce this","Supplement":"Sodium bicarbonate"},{"Boxing relevance":"Moderate — intramuscular carnosine buffering","Dosing":"3.2–6.4 g/day in divided doses for 4+ weeks","Evidence":"Reasonable","Practical notes":"Loading is cumulative, not acute — no point taking it on fight day. details: {"chapter_heading":"3. Recovery, Sleep and Load Management","groups":[{"blocks":[{"text":"Nothing else in this part comes close.","type":"text"},{"text":"The evidence: sleep extension research in athletes has demonstrated improvements in sprint performance and reaction time following extended sleep (Mah et al., 2011, in collegiate basketball players sleeping to 10 hours). Shorter sleep duration has been associated with substantially elevated injury risk — adolescent athletes sleeping under 8 hours showed markedly greater injury risk in Milewski et al. (2014). Slow-wave sleep is implicated in tissue repair and adaptation.","type":"text"},{"text":"For a boxer specifically, sleep also affects reaction time, decision-making, emotional regulation, and pain perception — all of which are boxing-critical, and all of which degrade before the athlete notices.","type":"text"},{"text":"3.1.1 The prescription","type":"subheading"},{"header":["Item","Prescription"],"rows":[{"Item":"Duration","Prescription":"8–10 hours per night during heavy training. This is a training variable, not a lifestyle preference"},{"Item":"Consistency","Prescription":"Same sleep and wake times, including weekends. Circadian regularity matters as much as duration"},{"Item":"Naps","Prescription":"20–40 min after morning sessions on two-a-day schedules. Genuinely valuable and standard among full-time fighters. Avoid naps longer than 40 min unless you can afford sleep inertia"},{"Item":"Environment","Prescription":"Cool (18–20 °C), dark, quiet"},{"Item":"Screens","Prescription":"None for 60 min pre-sleep"},{"Item":"Caffeine","Prescription":"Last dose 8+ hours before bed. Relevant if using caffeine pre-training"},{"Item":"Post-evening-training wind-down","Prescription":"Sympathetic arousal from a hard session takes 60–90 min to dissipate. Build the wind-down in: shower, food, low light, breathing practice, no screens"},{"Item":"Alcohol","Prescription":"Impairs sleep architecture, recovery, and adaptation. In a serious camp, zero"},{"Item":"Tracking","Prescription":"Duration and subjective quality daily. Treat a downward trend as seriously as a strength decline"}],"type":"table"},{"text":"3.1.2 Travel and jet lag","type":"subheading"},{"text":"For international competition: - Arrive one day per hour of time-zone shift before competing, where possible - Shift the sleep schedule 1 hour per day toward the destination time before departing - On arrival, adopt local meal and light timing immediately — light exposure is the strongest circadian signal - Avoid heavy training in the first 24 h; use light activity to entrain - Plan a specific hydration and food strategy for the flight","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"3.1 Sleep — the highest-return intervention available","order":1,"owner_rules":[{"changed_by":"Jason 2026-11-02 (D-PK74-4)","owner_source":"DOC-072 (Pro Boxing Skill System Master Registry, Workout_Map W-PHYS-06-A)","owner_text":["sleep opportunity, perceived fatigue, soreness, energy, mood/context, session quality, first technical failure, next training adjustment","Stop/regress when numbers become clearance rules, readiness thresholds, or medical interpretation"],"rule":"Sleep and recovery are logged with the owner's recovery-tracking fields, and the numbers never become clearance rules or readiness thresholds (the cells below). The Long Road prescription (duration, consistency, naps, environment, screens, caffeine, wind-down, alcohol, tracking) stays the starting default, overridable (RULES s0, s1)."}],"section":"LR-163","source":"LR-163 (The Long Road, Part 7, 3.1 Sleep — the highest-return intervention available)","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57)"},{"blocks":[{"header":["Modality","Evidence quality","Verdict for boxing"],"rows":[{"Evidence quality":"Strong","Modality":"Sleep","Verdict for boxing":"Priority one. Everything below is marginal by comparison"},{"Evidence quality":"Strong","Modality":"Nutrition and hydration","Verdict for boxing":"Priority two. Post-session refuelling determines the quality of tomorrow’s session"},{"Evidence quality":"Strong","Modality":"Load management","Verdict for boxing":"Priority three. The best recovery intervention is not needing to recover from an unnecessary session"},{"Evidence quality":"Moderate","Modality":"Active recovery (20–30 min low intensity)","Verdict for boxing":"Useful for perceived recovery and blood flow; low cost, low risk"},{"Evidence quality":"Effective acutely for soreness; attenuates resistance-training adaptations","Modality":"Cold water immersion","Verdict for boxing":"Periodize it — see §3.2.1"},{"Evidence quality":"Moderate for heat adaptation and plasma volume expansion","Modality":"Sauna / heat exposure","Verdict for boxing":"Useful in specific blocks. Never as a weight-cutting tool"},{"Evidence quality":"Weak for objective recovery, moderate for perceived recovery","Modality":"Massage / soft tissue work","Verdict for boxing":"Worth it if the athlete values it. Do not overstate the physiology"},{"Evidence quality":"Weak-moderate","Modality":"Compression garments","Verdict for boxing":"Low cost, low harm, small perceptual benefit"},{"Evidence quality":"Weak for soreness or performance","Modality":"Static stretching post-exercise","Verdict for boxing":"Do mobility work for range-of-motion goals, not as a recovery method"},{"Evidence quality":"Weak-moderate for perceived recovery and acute ROM","Modality":"Foam rolling","Verdict for boxing":"Cheap and harmless. Not a substitute for load management"},{"Evidence quality":"Weak or immature","Modality":"Cryotherapy chambers, red light, “recovery” devices, compression boots","Verdict for boxing":"Fine if free. Do not spend money here before you have fixed sleep"}],"type":"table"},{"text":"3.2.1 Cold water immersion — the periodization decision","type":"subheading"},{"text":"This deserves detail because it is widely used and widely mis-timed.","type":"text"},{"text":"What it does well: reduces perceived muscle soreness after acute high-intensity efforts, reduces markers of muscle damage and inflammation, and speeds recovery of muscle strength in the short term.","type":"text"},{"text":"What it costs: it attenuates the adaptations to resistance training. Roberts et al. (2015) found post-exercise CWI attenuated acute anabolic signalling and long-term adaptations in muscle to strength training. Fyfe et al. (2019) found CWI attenuated anabolic signalling and skeletal muscle fibre hypertrophy following whole-body resistance training — though notably not strength gain in that study. A meta-analysis by Piñero et al. (2024) examined post-exercise cold water immersion and resistance-training-induced hypertrophy and found effects that were likely small to negligible in some analyses; several narrative and meta-analytic reviews report that CWI following resistance training may blunt gains in absolute strength and muscular power. Evidence for negative effects on endurance training adaptations is much weaker.","type":"text"},{"text":"The periodized position (following Ihsan, Abbiss & Allan, 2021):","type":"text"},{"header":["Situation","Use CWI?"],"rows":[{"Situation":"After strength or power sessions during a development block","Use CWI?":"No. You are paying for adaptation with soreness relief"},{"Situation":"After sparring or high-intensity conditioning","Use CWI?":"Yes, if recovery for tomorrow matters more than adaptation from today"},{"Situation":"During intensified competition periods","Use CWI?":"Yes"},{"Situation":"Multi-day amateur tournaments","Use CWI?":"Yes — this is the clearest indication. Recovery for tomorrow’s bout unambiguously beats adaptation"},{"Situation":"After technical or aerobic sessions","Use CWI?":"Neutral; use if it helps perceived recovery"},{"Situation":"In the days immediately before competition","Use CWI?":"Yes, for perceived recovery"}],"type":"table"},{"text":"Protocol when used: 10–15 °C for 10–15 minutes. Note also that whole-body immersion close to bedtime may support sleep initiation via the core-temperature drop — a secondary benefit worth knowing during tournaments.","type":"text"},{"text":"Interesting supporting data for combat sport specifically: CWI enhanced wellness and 10 m sprint performance 24 h after simulated MMA combat, and reduced inflammation and oxidative stress after intense MMA training.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"3.2 Recovery modalities — an honest ranking","order":2,"owner_rules":[{"changed_by":"Jason 2026-11-02 (D-PK74-5)","owner_source":"DOC-027 (Punxsy Master Source Manual v1, Recovery and Regulation Source Manual v3, Post-Training Recovery Standard)","owner_text":["Use simple cooldown movement, light stretching where appropriate, walking, and controlled breathing."],"rule":"The session cool-down keeps the owner's downshift: simple cooldown movement, light stretching where appropriate, walking and controlled breathing. Needs Analysis: What the Sport Actually Demands","groups":[{"blocks":[{"text":"2.1.1 What the data say","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Multiple independent studies converge on a consistent profile.","type":"text"},{"text":"The 3 × 3-min format (current elite men’s and women’s format). In highly trained male amateur boxers undertaking a full-contact competitive bout, calculated energy provision was approximately:","type":"text"},{"text":"73% aerobic (oxidative)","type":"bullet"},{"text":"19% anaerobic alactic (phosphocreatine)","type":"bullet"},{"text":"8% anaerobic glycolytic","type":"bullet"},{"text":"with heart rate exceeding 93% of maximum in rounds 1 and 2 and above 97% in round 3, average oxygen uptake around 89% of VO₂max, and post-bout blood lactate above 15 mmol·L⁻¹ (range 12–18) (Bruzas et al., 2023). Note the striking detail in that study: the oxygen-uptake equivalent of total energy expenditure was calculated at approximately 122% of VO₂max — meaning the bout demands more energy per unit time than the boxer’s maximal aerobic power can supply, with the shortfall covered anaerobically.","type":"text"},{"text":"The 3 × 2-min format. A very similar distribution — roughly 77% aerobic, 19% phosphocreatine, 4% glycolytic (Davis et al., 2014).","type":"text"},{"text":"Elite Olympic boxers, simulated 3 × 3-min combat. Mean heart rates of 92%, 94% and 95% of maximum across rounds 1–3, with blood chemistry indicating marked acidosis (pH ≈ 7.21, bicarbonate ≈ 13 mmol·L⁻¹ after round 3).","type":"text"},{"text":"VO₂max values in elite Olympic boxers have been reported around 56 ml·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ for males and 50 for females — high, but not endurance-athlete high. This matters: the target is not a marathon runner’s engine, it is a large engine attached to a powerful, intermittent, skilled output.","type":"text"},{"text":"2.1.2 What this means mechanistically","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Understanding why the aerobic system dominates a sport that looks anaerobic is essential, because the intuition is wrong and the wrong intuition produces the wrong training.","type":"text"},{"text":"Why aerobic capacity dominates a 9-minute fight:","type":"text"},{"text":"1. Total energy demand over 9 minutes of work plus 2 minutes of recovery exceeds what anaerobic pathways can supply. Phosphocreatine stores are exhausted within seconds of maximal work. Glycolysis can run hard for tens of seconds to a couple of minutes before acidosis becomes performance-limiting. Nine minutes of near-continuous high-intensity work must therefore be predominantly oxidative, by arithmetic.","type":"text"},{"text":"2. Phosphocreatine resynthesis is an aerobic process. This is the single most important physiological fact in boxing conditioning. Every maximal punch, every explosive movement, draws on the phosphagen system — and refilling that system between actions, between exchanges, and between rounds depends on oxidative phosphorylation. A boxer with a bigger aerobic engine refills faster, and therefore can produce more maximal actions per round and enter round 3 with more available. Your aerobic system is not your “cardio.” It is your power supply’s recharging circuit.","type":"text"},{"text":"3. Lactate and hydrogen ion clearance is largely aerobic. Lactate is shuttled and oxidized. Better oxidative capacity means faster clearance during the low-intensity moments within a round and during the 60-second interval.","type":"text"},{"text":"4. Aerobic capacity determines the intensity you can sustain without accumulating acidosis. Two boxers with identical VO₂max but different lactate thresholds will fight at very different sustainable intensities.","type":"text"},{"text":"Why the alactic system is what wins: the actions that score and stop opponents — the maximal punch, the explosive entry, the sudden burst of three shots — are alactic. Notational data suggest that stoppages are typically preceded by sequences of high-force actions. So the alactic system’s power and its repeatability both matter, and repeatability is aerobically funded (see above).","type":"text"},{"text":"Why the glycolytic contribution is small but consequential: at 4–8% of total energy, glycolysis is not a major fuel source across a bout. But the hydrogen ions produced by high glycolytic flux are a primary fatigue mechanism. H⁺ accumulation interferes with the contractile process and with the enzymes of energy production, and it stimulates nerve endings producing the burning sensation and the perception of effort. Post-bout lactate above 15 mmol·L⁻¹ indicates very high glycolytic flux at points during the fight. Therefore buffering capacity — the ability to resist and clear acidosis — is a distinct trainable quality, separate from aerobic capacity, and it deserves its own dedicated training block.","type":"text"},{"text":"2.1.3 The three training implications (all of which contradict common gym practice)","type":"subheading"},{"text":"1. Aerobic capacity requires precise, monitored, progressive programming — not “roadwork.” It is not the thing you do to lose weight. It is the primary determinant of your ability to repeat maximal actions and recover between them.","type":"text"},{"text":"2. Long slow distance running is an inefficient tool for aerobic development in an already-trained athlete, and it interferes with power development. It has legitimate roles — early tissue conditioning, recovery, capillarization, psychological discipline — but the aerobic ceiling is raised far more efficiently by interval work. The concurrent training literature adds a further reason to limit running specifically: running produces more interference with strength adaptation than cycling, likely via eccentric loading and muscle damage.","type":"text"},{"text":"3. Buffering capacity needs its own block. You cannot get it as a side effect of aerobic work or of sparring. It requires repeated exposure to high acidosis with sufficient recovery to repeat the exposure at quality.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"2.1 Metabolic demands — the full picture","order":1,"section":"LR-013","source":"LR-013 (The Long Road, Part 1, 2.1 Metabolic demands — the full picture)","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"2.3.1 Activity profile","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Notational analysis of Olympic-level male boxing gives concrete behavioral targets:","type":"text"},{"text":"~1.4 discrete actions per second overall","type":"bullet"},{"text":"~20 punches per minute","type":"bullet"},{"text":"~2.5 defensive movements per minute","type":"bullet"},{"text":"~47 vertical hip movements per minute (i.e., continuous bouncing/level changing — roughly one every 1.3 seconds)","type":"bullet"},{"text":"(Davis, Wittekind & Beneke, 2013.)","type":"text"},{"text":"That hip-movement figure deserves attention. Nearly fifty vertical hip movements per minute is a continuous, rhythmic, whole-body activity underlying everything else — and it is metabolically expensive. It also degrades first when fatigue arrives, which is exactly what the bout-progression data show.","type":"text"},{"text":"2.3.2 What distinguishes winners from losers","type":"subheading"},{"text":"This is the most useful body of evidence in boxing performance analysis, and it says something coaches often resist.","type":"text"},{"text":"Elite male national championship bouts, ten-point must system (Thomson & Lamb, 2016), n = 26 elite males: - Winners’ hit rate: ~33%. Losers’: ~23%. - Winners’ air-punch rate (punches hitting nothing): ~17%. Losers’: ~27%. - Total punches thrown, total defensive actions, and interaction time did not differ meaningfully between winners and losers. - From rounds 1 to 2: clinch time increased, guard drops increased, bouncing decreased. Perceived fatigue effect rose throughout; perceived effort rose only from rounds 2 to 3.","type":"text"},{"text":"Elite women’s World Championship finals, 2023 (Ruggeri et al., 2025), 12 finals, 1,323 offensive and 1,456 defensive actions notated: - Winners performed fewer total offensive actions (635) than losers (688) - Winners’ offensive effectiveness ratio was significantly higher in every round (0.39 / 0.38 / 0.39 vs 0.26 / 0.28 / 0.29) - Winners landed more punches to the head specifically, and made greater use of rear-hand hooks and uppercuts - Pivoting and shifting back, particularly when followed by counterattack, were significantly associated with winning - Parrying and single counterpunches were associated with losing - Defensive effectiveness ratios also favored winners","type":"text"},{"text":"Earlier work (Davis et al., 2013) found that landing scoring punches was associated with maintaining a high frequency of attacking movement, particularly the lead-hand straight to the head followed by combinations, and that defensive movements are most valuable when they initiate a counterattack rather than merely avoid.","type":"text"},{"text":"Analysis of 2012 Olympic winners highlighted the predominance of straight punches and combinations, with higher accuracy and activity rates specifically in the final rounds.","type":"text"},{"text":"2.3.3 Translating this into training targets","type":"subheading"},{"header":["Finding","Training target"],"rows":[{"Finding":"Winners are more accurate, not busier","Training target":"Accuracy under pressure and under fatigue; shot selection; constrained sparring with accuracy scoring"},{"Finding":"Winners miss into air far less","Training target":"Range discipline — do not throw from outside your range. This is a distance skill, not a punching skill"},{"Finding":"Lead-hand straight to head is a primary scoring action","Training target":"Build five distinct jabs, each with its own intention and follow-up"},{"Finding":"Rear-hand hooks and uppercuts differentiate elite winners","Training target":"Do not neglect the rear-hand power hook and uppercut; most amateurs are jab-cross-only"},{"Finding":"Combinations score","Training target":"Combination architecture as a taught subject, not memorized flurries"},{"Finding":"Dynamic defense (pivot, shift-back) into counter wins; parrying and isolated single counters lose","Training target":"Every defensive action must be trained with an attached return. Layer defense: footwork first, head movement second, guard last"},{"Finding":"Accuracy and activity in the final round distinguishes winners","Training target":"Buffering capacity plus deliberately fatigued technical practice"},{"Finding":"Guard drops and bouncing loss appear by round 2","Training target":"Guard-integrity-under-fatigue as an explicit, measured KPI"}],"type":"table"},{"text":"The single most counterintuitive implication: “throw more punches” is bad advice. “Miss less, and counter off your defense” is the evidence-based instruction.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"2.3 Technical and tactical demands — what the winners actually do","order":2,"owner_rules":[{"changed_by":"Jason 2026-11-03 (D-PK82-7)","owner_source":"DOC-072 (Pro Boxing Skill System Master Registry, Skill_Index SKILL-06)","owner_text":["No dead defense; every defense exits or returns"],"rule":"Every defensive action is trained to end in an exit or a return (no dead defense). The Long Road's 'attached return' lines and its layering (footwork first, head movement second, guard last) stay as source text."}],"section":"LR-015","source":"LR-015 (The Long Road, Part 1, 2.3 Technical and tactical demands — what the winners actually do)","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57)"},{"backbone_differences":[{"backbone":null,"backbone_source":"no backbone record or catalog default carries either line (data/content/, design_catalogs.json and spine.json searched at the draft)","card":"B9-PK02-2","label":"decided at final review (Jason 2026-11-08, D-PK83-2-FR, A; ACTIONS A-60): one reading: at least 24 hours between hard sparring and a quality session; 48 hours is the more cautious choice; no new default","long_road":"hard sparring never sits within 24 hours of a session requiring cognitive or neuromuscular quality","reading":"One reading (Jason 2026-11-08, D-PK83-2-FR): keep at least 24 hours between hard sparring and a quality session (new technique, maximal strength or speed work); 48 hours, and spacing for any sparring, is the more cautious choice. LR-016 and LR-019 rule 4 stay verbatim on their groups; no new default; CONVENTION; LR-016's recovery-marker basis stays UNVERIFIED.","status":"INFERRED"}],"blocks":[{"text":"2.4.1 Musculoskeletal injury epidemiology","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Meta-analytic pooling of prospective amateur boxing data (Lystad et al., 2022, J Sci Med Sport, 17 cohorts) estimates:","type":"text"},{"text":"Competition injury incidence: ~54.7 per 1,000 athlete-exposures and ~6.8 per 1,000 minutes of exposure","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Training injury incidence: ~1.3 per 1,000 hours","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Translated: approximately one injury per 2.5 hours of competition, and one per 772 hours of training","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Most commonly injured regions: head and neck in competition (median ~72% of injuries); upper limb in training (median ~49%)","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Most common injuries: head and face contusions (competition), upper limb muscle strains (training)","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Injury incidence is lower in training than competition, but injury severity appears greater in training","type":"bullet"},{"text":"That last finding is the counterintuitive one, and it has a plausible explanation: competition injuries are dominated by contusions, which resolve quickly, whereas training injuries include the overuse and chronic problems — shoulders, hands, knees — that cost weeks or months.","type":"text"},{"text":"Hand and wrist specifically — longitudinal surveillance of the Great Britain Olympic squad, 2005–2012 (Loosemore et al., 2017): - Finger carpometacarpal instability and “boxer’s knuckle” (extensor hood and capsular injury at the metacarpophalangeal joint) were significantly more common than any other hand/wrist diagnosis - Competition hand/wrist injury rate: ~347 per 1,000 hours. Estimated training rate: <0.5 per 1,000 hours - The absolute number of injuries in training and competition was similar — remarkable given how vastly more hours are trained than competed","type":"text"},{"text":"Most debilitating (longest time-loss): shoulder and knee injuries. Supraspinatus pathology is the most commonly reported rotator cuff injury in amateur boxers.","type":"text"},{"text":"2.4.2 Head impact exposure and its consequences","type":"subheading"},{"text":"This is the section that shapes the entire system’s design, so it is presented in full.","type":"text"},{"text":"How much exposure does training produce? Instrumented mouthguard studies provide direct measurement. Jansen et al. (2021) recorded a mean of 42 ± 27 head impacts per male athlete and 32 ± 18 per female athlete during controlled two-minute sparring sessions — describing boxing practice as a source of substantial subconcussive impact doses. Extrapolate that: a boxer doing six two-minute rounds of sparring twice a week is plausibly absorbing several hundred head impacts weekly, and tens of thousands over a career, the overwhelming majority in the gym rather than in competition.","type":"text"},{"text":"What does a single sparring session do? Di Virgilio et al. (2019) studied 20 amateur boxers performing three 3-min sparring bouts, with a control group performing mock sparring, using transcranial magnetic stimulation, decomposition EMG, and memory tests. One hour post-sparring, boxers showed: - Increased corticomotor inhibition - Altered motor unit recruitment strategies - Decreased memory performance","type":"text"},{"text":"All returning to baseline at 24 hours. The authors interpret these as an acute GABAergic response, note the parallel with findings after football (soccer) heading, and observe that the changes resemble those seen following brain injury.","type":"text"},{"text":"Two things follow. First, the acute cost is real and measurable, not theoretical. Second, the recovery appears to occur within 24 hours on these markers — which is the basis for the rule in this system that hard sparring never sits within 24 hours of a session requiring cognitive or neuromuscular quality, but also a reason not to catastrophize any single session.","type":"text"},{"text":"Is there a threshold? Exploratory work monitoring symptoms alongside instrumented-mouthguard exposure in competitive boxers found no strong association between session exposure and symptom change at group level, but identified patterns in individual athletes, suggesting symptoms arose from combinations of high impact density, several above-average-magnitude impacts, and pre-existing individual predisposition. The authors argue explicitly for individual-specific analysis (Siegmund et al., 2026, J Sci Med Sport). Practical translation: there is no known safe dose, individual susceptibility varies, and population-level rules are less useful than individual monitoring.","type":"text"},{"text":"Long-term. In professional boxers, cumulative exposure to neurotrauma has been associated with impaired performance on cognitive processing measures (Bernick et al., 2014), and boxing has a long-documented association with chronic traumatic encephalopathy. Blood biomarker work in boxers has found neurofilament light (NFL) elevated 7–10 days post-bout and after three months of rest compared with controls, with higher elevations in boxers who took more than 15 head hits or experienced grogginess during or after a bout.","type":"text"},{"text":"Protective equipment and rules do work, partially. Scoping review evidence indicates that mandatory head guards together with modern thicker gloves significantly reduced knockout and head-injury rates in boxing, despite an increase in the number of head blows landed; that removing mandatory head guards significantly increased facial cuts; that mouthguards significantly reduced oral injuries; and that rule changes — shorter bouts, greater referee authority for standing counts, outclassed rules, medical stops — have reduced injury rates.","type":"text"},{"text":"2.4.3 The conclusion","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Not “don’t spar.” You cannot learn to fight without fighting, and no drill substitutes for a live opponent trying to hit you. The conclusion is:","type":"text"},{"text":"> Extract maximum learning per impact. Never take an impact that isn’t buying something no cheaper method could buy.","type":"text"},{"text":"This is operationalized as the eight-stage sparring continuum in Part 6 §9, with explicit weekly ceilings, progression criteria, and logging of head-impact exposure alongside sets and reps.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"2.4 Injury and trauma demands","order":3,"section":"LR-016","source":"LR-016 (The Long Road, Part 1, 2.4 Injury and trauma demands)","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57)"}],"owner_passages":[{"beside":["groups"],"common_errors":["Calling all hard work conditioning without identifying its purpose.","Using the same conditioning block regardless of training phase.","Mixing categories together until the athlete no longer knows the lesson."],"corrections":["Name the category before the block begins.","Keep the block tied to the day’s session purpose.","If the room loses behavior quality, downgrade the category before increasing motivation."],"difference":null,"doc":"DOC-027","doc_title":"Punxsy Master Source Manual v1","group":"LR-013","purpose":"Define the main categories of conditioning so coaches know what type of adaptation they are actually trying to create instead of calling every hard block conditioning.","read_for":"LR-013: DOC-027 §6_CondRecovery (Conditioning Category Structure; Burst to Reset Standard; Decision Under Fatigue Standard)","reading_note":"Beside 2.1.3: the owner's five categories name the adaptation each block seeks; the Long Road's aerobic, alactic and buffering qualities read across them (INFERRED: buffering work as Category 3 burst conditioning, as D-OQ55); no field filled; no disagreement drawn.","section":"Conditioning Category Structure","source_manual":"Conditioning and Energy System Source Manual v3","standards":["Category 1 is skill-conditioned work. The Physical Test Battery","groups":[{"blocks":[{"text":"The battery is adapted from validated boxing profiling work (Ruddock and colleagues; Boxing Science protocols) plus general S&C practice. The boxing-specific battery has demonstrated moderate-to-excellent test-retest reliability (ICC 0.7–0.9) and — importantly — discriminates senior from junior amateur boxers on press-ups, medicine ball throws, Yo-Yo IR1, countermovement jump, squat jump and 10 m sprint, which is the evidence that it measures something relevant rather than something merely measurable.","type":"text"},{"text":"Standardization rules that make the difference between data and noise: - Same time of day (±1 hour), same order, same equipment, same surface, same footwear - Same warm-up protocol, written down and followed exactly - At least 48 hours after hard training, never after sparring - Not in a state of acute weight loss - Three attempts on power tests, take the best; report all three so you can see variability - Record body mass at the same time, because most results are interpreted relative to it","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"2.1 Design logic","order":1,"section":"LR-028","source":"LR-028 (The Long Road, Part 2, 2.1 Design logic)","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57)"},{"backbone_differences":[{"backbone":"8x2min buffering <=10% decrement","backbone_source":"data/spine/spine.json stage T2 exit_gate (LR-055)","card":"B8-PK02-1","label":"decided at final review (Jason 2026-11-08, D-PK78-1-FR, A; ACTIONS A-60): the spine exit gates stay the values the app checks; the Long Road values are targets, shown as information","long_road":"4–6 × 2 min at a fixed high intensity","reading":"Long Road target (information): 4-6 x 2 min with a ≤10% decrement, beside the T2 exit gate value the app checks: 8 x 2 min with ≤10% decrement (Jason 2026-11-08, D-PK78-1-FR).","status":"INFERRED"}],"blocks":[{"text":"2.2.1 Body composition and anthropometry","type":"subheading"},{"header":["Measure","Protocol","Frequency","Interpretation"],"rows":[{"Frequency":"Daily","Interpretation":"Track 7-day rolling average, not single days","Measure":"Body mass","Protocol":"First thing, post-void, pre-food, same scale"},{"Frequency":"Every 6–12 weeks","Interpretation":"Track the raw sum in mm. Do not convert to body-fat percentage — the equations add error without adding information","Measure":"Sum of 7 skinfolds (ISAK sites: triceps, subscapular, biceps, supraspiliac, abdominal, front thigh, medial calf)","Protocol":"Same practitioner, same calipers, same order"},{"Frequency":"Once","Interpretation":"Determines your natural range and stylistic suitability","Measure":"Height, arm span, reach","Protocol":"Standard"},{"Frequency":"Every 12 weeks","Interpretation":"Detects where mass is gained or lost","Measure":"Girths: relaxed and flexed arm, thigh, calf, waist, chest","Protocol":"Tape, same sites"}],"type":"table"},{"text":"Why skinfold sum and not body-fat percentage: every body-fat equation was derived on a specific population and adds prediction error. The raw sum of skinfolds is a direct measurement with far better reliability, and for tracking change over time it is strictly better. If you want a single number to watch, watch that one.","type":"text"},{"text":"2.2.2 Lower-body power and reactive strength","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Countermovement jump (CMJ) - Protocol: hands on hips (to remove arm-swing variability) or with arm swing — pick one and never change. Stand tall, dip to self-selected depth, jump maximally. 3 attempts, 30–60 s rest, take best. - Measurement: force plate ideally; contact mat acceptable; validated phone app (e.g., using high-frame-rate video) acceptable for tracking. Jump height in cm. - Frequency: every 4–6 weeks for development tracking; and as a daily/weekly readiness marker (see §5). - Interpretation: untrained adult male ≈ 30–35 cm, female ≈ 22–27 cm. Well-trained boxer targets are in §2.3.","type":"text"},{"text":"Squat jump (SJ) - Protocol: squat to ~90° knee angle, hold for 3 seconds (this eliminates the stretch-shortening contribution), then jump maximally without any downward dip. 3 attempts. Any visible countermovement invalidates the rep. - Purpose: isolates concentric power, and — paired with CMJ — quantifies eccentric utilization. - The key derived metric: eccentric utilization ratio, or simply CMJ − SJ in cm. Recall that boxers characteristically show a very small difference (~0.9 cm reported average), some jumping higher in the SJ. A difference under 2 cm flags reactive strength as a priority. Target >4 cm.","type":"text"},{"text":"Drop jump reactive strength index (RSI) - Protocol: step off a box (start at 20 cm, progress to 30–40 cm only when competent), land and rebound as fast and high as possible. Instruction: “minimize your time on the ground, maximize your height.” 3–5 attempts. - Measurement: RSI = jump height ÷ ground contact time (or flight time ÷ contact time — pick one formula and keep it). - Introduce only when landing mechanics are competent. This test is a plyometric exposure, not just a measurement. - Interpretation: trained athletes commonly 1.5–2.5+ (using height/contact-time in m/s). What matters is your trend.","type":"text"},{"text":"2.2.3 Upper-body power","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Seated single-arm medicine ball “punch” throw — the most useful field proxy for punch force available without force-measuring equipment. - Protocol: seated on the floor with back against a wall (removes leg contribution) or seated on a bench (allows some trunk contribution — pick one). Ball at the shoulder in a punching position. Throw for maximum horizontal distance with a punching action. 3 attempts per arm. Measure to first contact point. - Ball mass: 3 kg for most, 4 kg for heavier boxers. Never change the ball mass between tests. - Track: lead-arm distance, rear-arm distance, and the asymmetry between them. Large asymmetry (>15–20%) is common and worth addressing. - Validity note: medicine ball throw distance correlates strongly with CMJ, SJ, press-up performance and sprint times, and moderately with lower-body lean mass — which is consistent with the kinetic-chain picture in Part 1 §2.2.","type":"text"},{"text":"Rotational medicine ball throw (optional addition): standing side-on to a wall, rotational throw for distance or for velocity if you have a radar/velocity device. Captures trunk rotational power specifically.","type":"text"},{"text":"2.2.4 Strength","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Maximal lower-body strength - Options, in order of preference for boxers: trap-bar deadlift 3–5RM; back squat 3–5RM; isometric mid-thigh pull peak force (if a force plate is available — best option, no fatigue cost, no technical failure mode). - Protocol for a 3–5RM: standardized warm-up ramp, then work to a set of 3–5 reps at a load you could not have completed 1–2 more reps with (RPE 8–9). Do not test true 1RM. The information gain is small and the risk and fatigue cost are not. - Report relative to body mass. “180 kg” is meaningless without “at 72 kg.” - Frequency: every 8–12 weeks, or estimate continuously from training loads using velocity or RPE data.","type":"text"},{"text":"Upper-body strength - Weighted chin-up 3–5RM (added mass as a percentage of body mass) — better than bench press as a boxing-relevant strength marker because pulling volume matters for shoulder health and posture - Bench press or floor press 3–5RM — track it, but recognize it as a general strength marker, not a punch-power predictor - Max strict press-ups, or press-ups in 60 s — validated in the boxing battery, discriminates seniors from juniors","type":"text"},{"text":"Cervical strength - Handheld dynamometer isometric peak force in flexion, extension, and lateral flexion left and right. Also useful: the ratio of flexion to extension, and left–right symmetry. - Every 8–12 weeks. Target ≥25% improvement from baseline in the first year, then maintenance.","type":"text"},{"text":"2.2.5 Speed","type":"subheading"},{"text":"5 m and 10 m sprint - Protocol: timing gates ideally (hand timing has too much error for 5 m). Standing start, front foot 30 cm behind the first gate. 3 attempts, full recovery. - Purpose: acceleration is the physical quality most similar to closing distance in the ring. - Frequency: every 8–12 weeks.","type":"text"},{"text":"2.2.6 Aerobic capacity","type":"subheading"},{"text":"30-15 Intermittent Fitness Test (30-15 IFT) — preferred - Protocol: 40 m shuttle course, 30 s of running interspersed with 15 s passive recovery, starting at 8 km·h⁻¹ and increasing 0.5 km·h⁻¹ per stage, paced by audio cues, to volitional exhaustion. - Output: VIFT — the velocity of the last completed stage. - Why preferred: it is intermittent, includes changes of direction and acceleration/deceleration, and — most usefully — it yields a directly prescribable velocity. You can then write conditioning sessions as percentages of VIFT rather than guessing. Comparative work in team-sport athletes has found the 30-15 IFT elicits higher VO₂max and maximal velocity values than treadmill protocols, reflecting its sport-specific demands.","type":"text"},{"text":"Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test Level 1 — good alternative - 2 × 20 m shuttles at increasing speed with 10 s active recovery. Validated in the boxing battery and discriminates senior from junior boxers.","type":"text"},{"text":"1200 m time trial — simple, equipment-free alternative - Maximal effort over 1200 m on a track. Crude, but repeatable and it correlates with the demands.","type":"text"},{"text":"Laboratory VO₂max and lactate profiling — best if accessible - Incremental treadmill or bike test with gas analysis and blood lactate sampling. Yields VO₂max, ventilatory thresholds, and — most usefully — the running speed or power at which lactate begins to accumulate (around 4 mmol·L⁻¹, though individual thresholds matter more than fixed values). This lets you prescribe conditioning with real precision.","type":"text"},{"text":"2.2.7 Anaerobic and repeat-effort capacity","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Repeated sprint test - Protocol: 6 × 35 m sprints with 10 s recovery (or 6 × 30 m with 20 s, or a bike equivalent). Record every time. - Key metric: percentage decrement = (total time ÷ (best time × number of sprints) − 1) × 100. A decrement under ~5% is good; over 8–10% indicates poor repeat-effort ability. - Why decrement matters more than best time: boxing does not require one fast sprint. It requires the twelfth burst to resemble the first.","type":"text"},{"text":"Buffering / acidosis tolerance assessment - Protocol: 4–6 × 2 min at a fixed high intensity (percentage of VIFT, or a fixed treadmill/bike setting) with 3 min recovery. Record distance or power per interval, and blood lactate after intervals 1, 3 and the final one if you have a lactate meter. - Interpretation: the shape of the decline across intervals, and the lactate values achieved and cleared. Target: sustaining output with ≤10% decrement while producing 12–14 mmol·L⁻¹.","type":"text"},{"text":"2.2.8 Mobility retest","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Repeat the §1.2 musculoskeletal screen every 8–12 weeks. Mobility that was adequate at baseline degrades under high training volume, particularly ankle dorsiflexion, hip internal rotation, and shoulder internal rotation.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"2.2 The battery in full","order":2,"section":"LR-029","source":"LR-029 (The Long Road, Part 2, 2.2 The battery in full)","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57)"},{"backbone_differences":[{"backbone":"CMJ +15-20%","backbone_source":"data/spine/spine.json stage T1 exit_gate (LR-045); also catalog gate pgt_b2023fc2fea6e0","card":"B8-PK02-1","label":"decided at final review (Jason 2026-11-08, D-PK78-1-FR, A; ACTIONS A-60): the spine exit gates stay the values the app checks; the Long Road values are targets, shown as information","long_road":"≥35 cm or +20%","reading":"Long Road target (information): Phase 1 exit CMJ '≥35 cm or +20%' (male), '≥27 cm or +20%' (female), beside the T1 exit gate value the app checks: CMJ +15-20% (Jason 2026-11-08, D-PK78-1-FR). (D-PK57 pattern; card TR-Q01 A)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"Purpose","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Define the standard session shape the system uses most often so coaches can plug in the right lesson without redesigning the delivery flow.","type":"text"},{"text":"Standards","type":"subheading"},{"text":"The base template is warm-up, activation, primary drill, integration block, finish block, and shutdown.","type":"text"},{"text":"Each phase should serve the same lesson chain rather than introducing unrelated topics.","type":"text"},{"text":"The primary drill is the center of the session and should receive the clearest attention and best energy.","type":"text"},{"text":"Watch Points","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Does the session move smoothly from readiness to main work to controlled application.","type":"text"},{"text":"Does the primary drill remain the center of the day.","type":"text"},{"text":"Does the finish block still reinforce the lesson instead of replacing it.","type":"text"},{"text":"Common Errors","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Over-expanding the integration block until it becomes a second session.","type":"text"},{"text":"Using the finish block to chase fatigue at the expense of the day’s lesson.","type":"text"},{"text":"Rushing the shutdown and losing the final learning anchor.","type":"text"},{"text":"Corrections and Responses","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Protect the base flow unless a strong reason exists to change it.","type":"text"},{"text":"If time compresses, shorten support blocks before cutting the primary drill.","type":"text"},{"text":"If the lesson is fragile, reduce integration complexity rather than expanding explanation.","type":"text"},{"text":"Use Case","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Use for most technical and developmental sessions across the program.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"Base 60 Minute Session Template","order":5,"section":"DOC-027 Session Templates and Weekly Build Patterns Source Manual v3, section 5","source":"DOC-027 (Punxsy Master Source Manual v1, Session Templates and Weekly Build Patterns Source Manual v3; compiled from the DOC-028 v3 set), 'Base 60 Minute Session Template'","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57 pattern; card TR-Q01 A)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"Purpose","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Define the template for days where the room must build or sharpen the most important current skill behavior under high attention and controlled stress.","type":"text"},{"text":"Standards","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Keep warm-up and activation tightly linked to the main skill.","type":"text"},{"text":"Use one primary drill with high repetition quality.","type":"text"},{"text":"Use one controlled integration picture only if the main behavior is stable enough to transfer.","type":"text"},{"text":"Finish with a short precise reinforcement rather than a broad fatigue block.","type":"text"},{"text":"Watch Points","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Is the room attentive enough to absorb technical refinement.","type":"text"},{"text":"Is the coach protecting repetition quality.","type":"text"},{"text":"Does the finish block still look like the same lesson.","type":"text"},{"text":"Common Errors","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Turning hard skill day into hard everything day.","type":"text"},{"text":"Adding extra topics because the room looks motivated.","type":"text"},{"text":"Letting fatigue blur the exact skill being installed.","type":"text"},{"text":"Corrections and Responses","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Shorten total density if focus quality starts dropping.","type":"text"},{"text":"Protect the main drill above all secondary additions.","type":"text"},{"text":"End while the room is still producing clean usable reps.","type":"text"},{"text":"Use Case","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Use for core correction days, installation phases, and early-week anchor work.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"Hard Skill Day Template","order":6,"section":"DOC-027 Session Templates and Weekly Build Patterns Source Manual v3, section 6","source":"DOC-027 (Punxsy Master Source Manual v1, Session Templates and Weekly Build Patterns Source Manual v3; compiled from the DOC-028 v3 set), 'Hard Skill Day Template'","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57 pattern; card TR-Q01 A)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"Purpose","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Define the template for days where the room should stabilize an already taught behavior across slightly changing pictures without changing the system lesson.","type":"text"},{"text":"Standards","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Start with a shorter reinstall of the core behavior.","type":"text"},{"text":"Move into one support picture that demands the same decision in a different form.","type":"text"},{"text":"Use controlled live or game-like exposure only if the original cue still holds.","type":"text"},{"text":"Watch Points","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Does the support picture reinforce rather than widen the lesson.","type":"text"},{"text":"Can athletes still respond to the same cue under the second picture.","type":"text"},{"text":"Is the room learning transfer or only collecting variation.","type":"text"},{"text":"Common Errors","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Using reinforcement day to introduce a whole new idea.","type":"text"},{"text":"Adding so much variation that the core lesson disappears.","type":"text"},{"text":"Failing to compare the support picture back to the main behavior.","type":"text"},{"text":"Corrections and Responses","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Keep the same cue family across both blocks.","type":"text"},{"text":"If the second picture breaks the lesson, return to the cleaner one immediately.","type":"text"},{"text":"Use less variation when transfer is fragile.","type":"text"},{"text":"Use Case","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Use for midweek stabilization, post-installation work, and pre-sparring sharpening.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"Reinforcement Day Template","order":7,"section":"DOC-027 Session Templates and Weekly Build Patterns Source Manual v3, section 7","source":"DOC-027 (Punxsy Master Source Manual v1, Session Templates and Weekly Build Patterns Source Manual v3; compiled from the DOC-028 v3 set), 'Reinforcement Day Template'","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57 pattern; card TR-Q01 A)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"Purpose","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Define the template for days where the room must preserve movement quality, confidence, and continuity while reducing total stress load.","type":"text"},{"text":"Standards","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Use easier entry into movement, lighter technical patterning, lower emotional load, and short clear blocks.","type":"text"},{"text":"The purpose is to leave the athlete more organized, not more exhausted.","type":"text"},{"text":"The lesson should still exist, but the demand should not threaten recovery.","type":"text"},{"text":"Watch Points","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Do athletes look calmer and cleaner as the session goes on.","type":"text"},{"text":"Does the room stay honest about the day being recovery-oriented.","type":"text"},{"text":"Are athletes trying to turn maintenance into competition.","type":"text"},{"text":"Common Errors","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Sneaking hard conditioning or heavy live work into a recovery template.","type":"text"},{"text":"Talking too much because the work looks lighter.","type":"text"},{"text":"Allowing the room tone to become too loose and lose structure.","type":"text"},{"text":"Corrections and Responses","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Keep the session shorter and cleaner if needed.","type":"text"},{"text":"Use stable familiar drill pictures.","type":"text"},{"text":"Re-state that the value of the day is quality restoration, not emotional satisfaction.","type":"text"},{"text":"Use Case","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Use on planned recovery days, post-sparring recovery, and high-stress weeks.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"Recovery and Technical Maintenance Template","order":8,"section":"DOC-027 Session Templates and Weekly Build Patterns Source Manual v3, section 8","source":"DOC-027 (Punxsy Master Source Manual v1, Session Templates and Weekly Build Patterns Source Manual v3; compiled from the DOC-028 v3 set), 'Recovery and Technical Maintenance Template'","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57 pattern; card TR-Q01 A)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"Purpose","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Define the template for days when the room should sharpen timing, cue readiness, and confidence without creating fatigue or new confusion.","type":"text"},{"text":"Standards","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Use short familiar sequences and familiar cue language.","type":"text"},{"text":"Keep the session crisp, low-volume, and highly recognizable.","type":"text"},{"text":"The athlete should leave feeling sharp and clear, not tested.","type":"text"},{"text":"Watch Points","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Does the athlete look faster and cleaner without strain.","type":"text"},{"text":"Is the coach resisting the temptation to fix late details.","type":"text"},{"text":"Does the room finish before quality starts flattening.","type":"text"},{"text":"Common Errors","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Adding new tactics on primer day.","type":"text"},{"text":"Extending the session because the room looks fresh.","type":"text"},{"text":"Using hard conditioning because the session felt too easy.","type":"text"},{"text":"Corrections and Responses","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Cut volume before the room goes flat.","type":"text"},{"text":"Protect familiar successful pictures.","type":"text"},{"text":"Use one final confidence anchor before shutdown.","type":"text"},{"text":"Use Case","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Use before sparring anchors, before competition, and in taper phases.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"Primer Template","order":9,"section":"DOC-027 Session Templates and Weekly Build Patterns Source Manual v3, section
