the record (D-PK57 pattern; card TR-Q01 A)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"Purpose","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Define the most common week pattern so coaches can place templates in a useful order instead of improvising the week every time.","type":"text"},{"text":"Standards","type":"subheading"},{"text":"A common pattern is hard skill, recovery, reinforcement, primer, sparring anchor, optional support, off day.","type":"text"},{"text":"The exact day names may shift, but the weekly roles should remain visible.","type":"text"},{"text":"The most stressful days should not cluster without reason.","type":"text"},{"text":"Watch Points","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Does the week move from build to restore to reapply to sharpen to test.","type":"text"},{"text":"Is the sparring day protected by the surrounding schedule.","type":"text"},{"text":"Does the week still have a recovery identity and an anchor identity.","type":"text"},{"text":"Common Errors","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Calling every session equally important and equally hard.","type":"text"},{"text":"Losing weekly rhythm due to random changes.","type":"text"},{"text":"Placing the hardest conditioning or most chaotic work too close to the anchor day.","type":"text"},{"text":"Corrections and Responses","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Keep the weekly roles visible even when days shift.","type":"text"},{"text":"If the week compresses, keep the key roles and remove secondary additions.","type":"text"},{"text":"Protect the recovery day and the anchor day first.","type":"text"},{"text":"Use Case","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Use for recurring weekly planning and short camps.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"Weekly Build Pattern habit-based.","type":"text"},{"text":"Standards","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Select the template based on the current need: install, reinforce, restore, sharpen, or test.","type":"text"},{"text":"The athlete’s readiness, attendance continuity, fatigue state, and weekly position should all matter.","type":"text"},{"text":"The template should serve the lesson, not the coach’s favorite style of session.","type":"text"},{"text":"Watch Points","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Does the day need learning, transfer, restoration, or readiness.","type":"text"},{"text":"Is the athlete prepared for the chosen template’s demand level.","type":"text"},{"text":"Would a simpler template produce a better lesson today.","type":"text"},{"text":"Common the week needs it.","type":"text"},{"text":"Ignoring disruption in attendance or fatigue and forcing the ideal template anyway.","type":"text"},{"text":"Corrections and Responses","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Ask what the day is for before choosing the shape.","type":"text"},{"text":"Use the least complex template that still solves the need.","type":"text"},{"text":"If the room is unstable, select a cleaner template and rebuild.","type":"text"},{"text":"Use Case","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Use during weekly planning, day-of details: {"chapter_heading":null,"field_provenance":"PPBF source manual v3","groups":[{"blocks":[{"text":"This file defines how the coaching system scales drills, sessions, and live demands across different athlete readiness levels without changing core identity.","type":"text"},{"text":"It is a neutral source file. It is not written for one athlete, one opponent, or one event.","type":"text"},{"text":"Its purpose is to let one room run one system across different levels while protecting clarity, safety, and transfer.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"Document Purpose","order":1,"section":"DOC-027 Scaling and Progression Source Manual v3, section 1","source":"DOC-027 (Punxsy Master Source Manual v1, Scaling and Progression Source Manual v3; compiled from the DOC-028 v3 set), 'Document Purpose'","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57 pattern; card TR-Q01 A)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"Athletes should progress by proving decision quality, structure, and composure under the current demand level before moving to a harder one.","type":"text"},{"text":"Progression is not earned by surviving chaos, showing toughness, or asking for harder work.","type":"text"},{"text":"Regression is not failure. Regression is a tool for restoring the target behavior.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"Primary Progression Principle","order":2,"section":"DOC-027 Scaling and Progression Source Manual v3, section 2","source":"DOC-027 (Punxsy Master Source Manual v1, Scaling and Progression Source Manual v3; compiled from the DOC-028 v3 set), 'Primary Progression Principle'","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57 pattern; card TR-Q01 A)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"Same drill, same lesson, different demand.","type":"text"},{"text":"Scaling must preserve the system, not create a second system.","type":"text"},{"text":"Harder is only better if the target behavior still appears.","type":"text"},{"text":"If a higher version removes the intended behavior, it is the wrong version.","type":"text"},{"text":"Progression should add decision demand before adding disorder or fatigue.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"Non Negotiable Progression Rules","order":3,"section":"DOC-027 Scaling and Progression Source Manual v3, section 3","source":"DOC-027 (Punxsy Master Source Manual v1, Scaling and Progression Source Manual v3; compiled from the DOC-028 v3 set), 'Non Negotiable Progression Rules'","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57 pattern; card TR-Q01 A)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"A, B, and C scaling definitions.","type":"text"},{"text":"When coaches should progress or regress a drill.","type":"text"},{"text":"How week-to-week training demand should rise or fall.","type":"text"},{"text":"How mixed-level rooms can stay on one lesson.","type":"text"},{"text":"How to identify whether an athlete needs installation, reinforcement, or progression.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"What This File Controls","order":4,"section":"DOC-027 Scaling and Progression Source Manual v3, section 4","source":"DOC-027 (Punxsy Master Source Manual v1, Scaling and Progression Source Manual v3; compiled from the DOC-028 v3 set), 'What This File Controls'","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57 pattern; card TR-Q01 A)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"Purpose","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Define the three standard versions of a drill so coaches can keep one room on one lesson without turning the room into multiple different programs.","type":"text"},{"text":"Standards","type":"subheading"},{"text":"A means easier and controlled success. The drill picture is simplified so the athlete can feel and repeat the target behavior cleanly.","type":"text"},{"text":"B means fight level or standard system level. The drill picture matches the intended real demand without extra decoration.","type":"text"},{"text":"C means harder than fight. The drill picture adds stress, delay, variation, or disruption, but must still preserve the same lesson.","type":"text"},{"text":"All three versions must teach the same rule, use the same cue family, and end with the same behavioral goal.","type":"text"},{"text":"Coach Watch Points","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Does the athlete understand the target behavior at the current level.","type":"text"},{"text":"Can the athlete still respond to one cue.","type":"text"},{"text":"Does the harder version still display the same lesson or has it changed the problem entirely.","type":"text"},{"text":"Is the coach accidentally using C because it looks advanced rather than because it is useful.","type":"text"},{"text":"Common Errors","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Treating A like beginner work only and therefore beneath better athletes.","type":"text"},{"text":"Treating B as automatic even when the athlete is not ready for it.","type":"text"},{"text":"Treating C as a reward rather than a test of retained structure.","type":"text"},{"text":"Using different cues at each level and confusing the room.","type":"text"},{"text":"Corrections and Responses","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Move to A when the cue is not holding, the athlete is rushing, or the room is too noisy for the lesson to land.","type":"text"},{"text":"Stay at B when the athlete can solve the intended picture under normal live demand without drift.","type":"text"},{"text":"Move to C only when B is stable and the coach wants to confirm that the target behavior survives added complexity.","type":"text"},{"text":"If C changes the lesson, redesign the constraint instead of pushing through.","type":"text"},{"text":"Use Case","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Use every time multiple levels are present in the same room or when an athlete is oscillating between control and breakdown.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"A / B / C Scale Definitions","order":5,"section":"DOC-027 Scaling and Progression Source Manual v3, section 5","source":"DOC-027 (Punxsy Master Source Manual v1, Scaling and Progression Source Manual v3; compiled from the DOC-028 v3 set), 'A / B / C Scale Definitions'","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57 pattern; card TR-Q01 A)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"Purpose","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Define the three main teaching states so the coach knows whether the athlete needs first exposure, repeated consolidation, or an increase in decision demand.","type":"text"},{"text":"Standards","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Installation means the athlete is still learning what the correct behavior feels like and looks like.","type":"text"},{"text":"Reinforcement means the athlete has seen the right behavior but cannot yet hold it consistently across different pictures.","type":"text"},{"text":"Progression means the athlete can hold the target behavior reliably enough that added demand can now test the behavior rather than erase it.","type":"text"},{"text":"Coach Watch Points","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Does the athlete know the correct action only when it is pre-called.","type":"text"},{"text":"Can the athlete still find the target behavior when the picture changes slightly.","type":"text"},{"text":"Does the athlete recover after one mistake or fully lose the lesson.","type":"text"},{"text":"Is the athlete stable enough that a harder version will teach something real instead of simply exposing collapse.","type":"text"},{"text":"Common Errors","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Progressing too early because the athlete looked good in one clean set.","type":"text"},{"text":"Reinforcing forever because the coach is uncomfortable adding any uncertainty.","type":"text"},{"text":"Calling something progression when it is really random difficulty.","type":"text"},{"text":"Using volume instead of better progression steps.","type":"text"},{"text":"Corrections and Responses","type":"subheading"},{"text":"If the athlete cannot show the target behavior twice in a row, return to installation logic.","type":"text"},{"text":"If the athlete can perform the behavior only in one picture, remain in reinforcement.","type":"text"},{"text":"If the athlete can solve the behavior across small changes and remain coachable, progression can begin.","type":"text"},{"text":"Use one progression variable at a time so cause and effect stay visible.","type":"text"},{"text":"Use Case","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Use for weekly planning, assistant-coach decisions, and post-session review when deciding what the next session should do.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"Installation vs Reinforcement vs Progression","order":6,"section":"DOC-027 Scaling and Progression Source Manual v3, section 6","source":"DOC-027 (Punxsy Master Source Manual v1, Scaling and Progression Source Manual v3; compiled from the DOC-028 v3 set), 'Installation vs Reinforcement vs Progression'","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57 pattern; card TR-Q01 A)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"Purpose","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Provide a neutral menu of variables that coaches can change without redesigning the drill or losing the lesson.","type":"text"},{"text":"Standards","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Entry predictability can be reduced or increased.","type":"text"},{"text":"Target stability can be reduced or increased.","type":"text"},{"text":"Partner movement can be simplified or made more variable.","type":"text"},{"text":"Decision delay can be shortened or lengthened.","type":"text"},{"text":"Disruption can be added or removed.","type":"text"},{"text":"Fatigue can be added only after the main decision pattern is stable.","type":"text"},{"text":"Coach Watch Points","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Which variable is actually causing the athlete to fail.","type":"text"},{"text":"Whether the coach is changing too many variables at once.","type":"text"},{"text":"Whether a new variable adds the intended stress or merely makes the rep messy.","type":"text"},{"text":"Whether the athlete still knows what the drill is teaching.","type":"text"},{"text":"Common Errors","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Adding movement, disruption, and live response all at once.","type":"text"},{"text":"Using fatigue as the first progression tool.","type":"text"},{"text":"Letting partner unpredictability rise faster than athlete understanding.","type":"text"},{"text":"Mistaking visual complexity for real decision progression.","type":"text"},{"text":"Corrections and Responses","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Change one variable and observe the result before changing a second.","type":"text"},{"text":"If a new variable destroys the cue, pull it back immediately.","type":"text"},{"text":"Build progression from clean picture to changing picture to pressured picture to disrupted picture.","type":"text"},{"text":"Use fatigue last, not first.","type":"text"},{"text":"Use Case","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Use when converting a primary drill into a fight-relevant progression without losing the original lesson.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"Drill Progression Variables","order":7,"section":"DOC-027 Scaling and Progression Source Manual v3, section 7","source":"DOC-027 (Punxsy Master Source Manual v1, Scaling and Progression Source Manual v3; compiled from the DOC-028 v3 set), 'Drill Progression Variables'","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57 pattern; card TR-Q01 A)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"Purpose","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Define how training demand should rise across a short camp or training block without changing the program identity.","type":"text"},{"text":"Standards","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Week one emphasizes installation and behavioral clarity.","type":"text"},{"text":"Week two usually adds more movement or timing stress while preserving control.","type":"text"},{"text":"Week three often adds disruption or recovery-under-pressure work.","type":"text"},{"text":"Week four usually carries the highest specific live relevance, not the highest random chaos.","type":"text"},{"text":"Week five or taper periods reduce total load while preserving speed, timing, and confidence.","type":"text"},{"text":"Coach Watch Points","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Does each week add a useful type of stress rather than just more stress.","type":"text"},{"text":"Is the room carrying too many unfinished lessons into the next week.","type":"text"},{"text":"Are live demands rising faster than behavior reliability.","type":"text"},{"text":"Is the athlete entering later weeks overloaded instead of sharpened.","type":"text"},{"text":"Common Errors","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Increasing intensity every week just because a camp is progressing.","type":"text"},{"text":"Adding new lessons late because the coach notices a flaw and panics.","type":"text"},{"text":"Failing to reduce load near the end because the athlete looks strong.","type":"text"},{"text":"Confusing specific stress with chaotic stress.","type":"text"},{"text":"Corrections and Responses","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Raise stress by changing one main variable per phase: clarity, movement, disruption, live specificity, then simplification.","type":"text"},{"text":"If the athlete is not holding the current layer, keep the same week theme but reduce the live demand.","type":"text"},{"text":"Late camp weeks should become clearer, not noisier.","type":"text"},{"text":"When in doubt, sharpen what already exists instead of adding.","type":"text"},{"text":"Use Case","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Use for five-week camps, short competition runs, and developmental blocks that need clear phase logic.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"Week to Week Progression Control","order":8,"section":"DOC-027 Scaling and Progression Source Manual v3, section 8","source":"DOC-027 (Punxsy Master Source Manual v1, Scaling and Progression Source Manual v3; compiled from the DOC-028 v3 set), 'Week to Week Progression Control'","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57 pattern; card TR-Q01 A)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"Purpose","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Define how one room can contain multiple athlete levels without losing the system or fracturing into unrelated drills and private coaching worlds.","type":"text"},{"text":"Standards","type":"subheading"},{"text":"All athletes should stay on the same lesson even if demand differs.","type":"text"},{"text":"The cue family should remain the same across A, B, and C.","type":"text"},{"text":"The lead coach should be able to explain the room theme in one sentence to everyone.","type":"text"},{"text":"Assistant coaches can manage different versions but not different purposes.","type":"text"},{"text":"Coach Watch Points","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Are weaker athletes being protected without being isolated from the lesson.","type":"text"},{"text":"Are advanced athletes still being challenged without drifting from the system.","type":"text"},{"text":"Do assistants understand which part of the drill may change and which part must stay the same.","type":"text"},{"text":"Can the room still identify the day’s main rule.","type":"text"},{"text":"Common Errors","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Running three different lessons at once.","type":"text"},{"text":"Using advanced athletes as proof that the system is harder than it really needs to be.","type":"text"},{"text":"Giving newer athletes so little live information that they never learn to transfer the skill.","type":"text"},{"text":"Letting stronger athletes freeload into chaos because they are capable.","type":"text"},{"text":"Corrections and Responses","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Keep the main drill the same and vary only the demand picture.","type":"text"},{"text":"Give each group one or two allowable constraints, not a full new plan.","type":"text"},{"text":"Require all groups to finish under the same behavioral standard.","type":"text"},{"text":"If the room is splitting conceptually, regroup and restate the lesson before continuing.","type":"text"},{"text":"Use Case","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Use in busy classes, mixed-age sessions, and any session with both developing and advanced athletes present.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"Mixed Level Room Management","order":9,"section":"DOC-027 Scaling and Progression Source Manual v3, section 9","source":"DOC-027 (Punxsy Master demand.","type":"text"},{"text":"Standards","type":"subheading"},{"text":"The athlete can repeat the target behavior with one cue only.","type":"text"},{"text":"The athlete can recover after one mistake without forgetting the lesson.","type":"text"},{"text":"The athlete can maintain balance, breathing, and visual control during the drill.","type":"text"},{"text":"The athlete can finish the rep without creating a new avoidable problem.","type":"text"},{"text":"The athlete is not using speed to hide confusion.","type":"text"},{"text":"Coach Watch Points","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Does the athlete need repeated rescue.","type":"text"},{"text":"Is the athlete still reacting emotionally under mild pressure.","type":"text"},{"text":"Can the athlete still arrive in stance after the behavior is performed.","type":"text"},{"text":"Does the athlete know why the rep succeeded.","type":"text"},{"text":"Common Errors","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Progressing based on effort alone.","type":"text"},{"text":"Progressing because the athlete is bored.","type":"text"},{"text":"Progressing because the room is ahead of schedule.","type":"text"},{"text":"Progressing when the athlete still depends on heavy coach guidance.","type":"text"},{"text":"Corrections and Responses","type":"subheading"},{"text":"If two or more readiness gates are missing, do not progress.","type":"text"},{"text":"If the athlete loses one gate only under live work, keep the drill but simplify the picture.","type":"text"},{"text":"If the athlete retains all gates consistently, It is not tied to one athlete, one opponent, or one event.","type":"text"},{"text":"Its purpose is to make drill assignment faster, clearer, and more system-consistent by creating a canonical problem-to-response lookup structure.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"Document Purpose","order":1,"section":"DOC-040 Drill Assignment Matrix Source Manual v3, section 1","source":"DOC-040 (Punxsy_Drill_Assignment_Matrix_Source_v3.docx, Library Intake/R04 - Coaching and Coach Development), 'Document Purpose'","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57 pattern; Jason 2026-11-09 (D-OQ195))"},{"blocks":[{"text":"The matrix should solve the earliest useful break in the chain, not only the loudest visible error.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"A good matrix narrows choices instead of generating more options than the coach can use.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Each mapped response should stay inside the same core system rules.","type":"bullet"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"Primary Matrix Principle","order":2,"section":"DOC-040 Drill Assignment Matrix Source Manual v3, section 2","source":"DOC-040 (Punxsy_Drill_Assignment_Matrix_Source_v3.docx, Library Intake/R04 - Coaching and Coach Development), 'Primary Matrix Principle'","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57 pattern; Jason 2026-11-09 (D-OQ195))"},{"blocks":[{"text":"Name the athlete’s main current failure pattern in behavior language.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Identify whether the break is entry, position, decision, finish, reset, composure, read, or recovery related.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Select the primary drill family that targets that exact link first.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Select one cue family only.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Assign one sparring role or live picture that tests the corrected behavior.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Choose one regression and one progression option in advance.","type":"bullet"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"How the Matrix Should Be Used","order":3,"section":"DOC-040 Drill Assignment Matrix Source Manual v3, section 3","source":"DOC-040 (Punxsy_Drill_Assignment_Matrix_Source_v3.docx, Library Intake/R04 - Coaching and Coach Development), 'How the Matrix Should Be Used'","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57 pattern; Jason 2026-11-09 (D-OQ195))"},{"blocks":[{"text":"Stays too long after scoring -> Touch to Reposition, 3 and Out, Finish Clean.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Chases retreat or movement -> Structured Pursuit, Calm Pressure, Win the Edges.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Loses shape after contact or interruption -> Post Hit Reset, Break Set Score.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Fights in disorder instead of leaving -> Chaos Recognition, Better Spot exit drills.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Cannot solve long guard or barrier picture -> Long Guard Entry, line-change entry drills.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Bad edge behavior or poor ring location -> Win the Edges, lane-control and ring-cut drills.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Poor read quality or guessing -> Perceptual ladder drills, read-first counter drills.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Late defensive recognition -> Defense and Reposition drills, early-recognition defense blocks.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Greedy continuation after success -> capped-exchange drills, Finish and Leave, 3 and Out.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Freezes or loses composure under pressure -> reset ladders, composure drills, controlled disruption blocks.","type":"bullet"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"Core Failure Pattern to Drill Family Mapping","order":4,"section":"DOC-040 Drill Assignment Matrix Source Manual v3, section 4","source":"DOC-040 (Punxsy_Drill_Assignment_Matrix_Source_v3.docx, Library Intake/R04 - Coaching and Coach Development), 'Core Failure Pattern to Drill Family Mapping'","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57 pattern; Jason 2026-11-09 (D-OQ195))"},{"blocks":[{"text":"Position problems usually map first to feet first, better spot, own the ground, or cut first.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Finish problems usually map first to three and out, finish and leave, or nothing extra.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Reset problems usually map first to reset, back to shape, or see first.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Read problems usually map first to see first, make him show it, or do not bite.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Composure problems usually map first to breathe, stay clean, or slow down.","type":"bullet"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"Cue Family Mapping Rules","order":5,"section":"DOC-040 Drill Assignment Matrix Source Manual v3, section 5","source":"DOC-040 (Punxsy_Drill_Assignment_Matrix_Source_v3.docx, Library Intake/R04 - Coaching and Coach Development), 'Cue Family Mapping Rules'","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57 pattern; Jason 2026-11-09 (D-OQ195))"},{"blocks":[{"text":"Retreat-chase problems -> retreat role, delay role, edge-denial role.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Disruption problems -> clinch-break role, crowding role, interruption role.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Read and timing problems -> delayed-output role, rhythm-break role, false-open role.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Space-control problems -> ring-cut role, edge-pressure role, lane-denial role.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Composure problems -> controlled-chaos role with early downgrade triggers.","type":"bullet"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"Sparring Role Mapping Rules","order":6,"section":"DOC-040 Drill Assignment Matrix Source Manual v3, section 6","source":"DOC-040 (Punxsy_Drill_Assignment_Matrix_Source_v3.docx, Library Intake/R04 - Coaching and Coach Development), 'Sparring Role Mapping Rules'","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57 pattern; Jason 2026-11-09 (D-OQ195))"},{"blocks":[{"text":"Regression should remove noise while preserving the same lesson.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Progression should add one variable only: movement, delay, disruption, read complexity, or mild fatigue.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"If the athlete loses the cue, return to the last clean matrix level immediately.","type":"bullet"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"Regression and Progression Standard","order":7,"section":"DOC-040 Drill Assignment Matrix Source Manual v3, section 7","source":"DOC-040 (Punxsy_Drill_Assignment_Matrix_Source_v3.docx, Library Intake/R04 - Coaching and Coach Development), 'Regression and Progression Standard'","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57 pattern; Jason 2026-11-09 (D-OQ195))"},{"blocks":[{"text":"Choosing drills from personal preference rather than chain logic.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Assigning too many drills to one problem.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Changing cue families while keeping the same problem.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Using a sparring role that does not actually test the corrected behavior.","type":"bullet"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"Common Matrix Errors","order":8,"section":"DOC-040 Drill Assignment Matrix Source Manual v3, section 8","source":"DOC-040 (Punxsy_Drill_Assignment_Matrix_Source_v3.docx, Library Intake/R04 - Coaching and Coach Development), 'Common Matrix Errors'","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57 pattern; details: {"chapter_heading":"5. The Fifteen Most Common Pitfalls","groups":[{"blocks":[{"text":"Ranked roughly by how much damage they do.","type":"text"},{"text":"1. Sparring too hard, too often, too early. The single most damaging error in the sport. It stunts skill development (you cannot learn while surviving), shortens careers, and causes permanent harm. Every other item on this list is recoverable.","type":"text"},{"text":"2. Ignoring or hiding concussion symptoms. The error that causes irreversible damage. There is no version of courage that includes it.","type":"text"},{"text":"3. Chronic weight cutting. Degrades performance, health, and career length. If you cut more than 5%, you are in the wrong class. The evidence in amateur multi-day tournaments specifically shows weight regain is not linked to success.","type":"text"},{"text":"4. Competing before ready. A first bout at four months produces a bad experience, a set of panic habits, and often a lost boxer.","type":"text"},{"text":"5. Skipping the technical foundation to get to “the fun stuff.” Ceilings installed in year one cannot be removed in year five, because pressure reveals the earliest-learned pattern.","type":"text"},{"text":"6. Practising in unrepresentative conditions. Choreographed pad work with a cooperative coach develops the skill of hitting pads. It has a place; it is not where fight skill is built.","type":"text"},{"text":"7. Avoiding heavy strength training. The evidence directly contradicts the fear. Lower-body maximal strength is associated with punch impact force, and 84% of practitioners acknowledge this while programming it least.","type":"text"},{"text":"8. Endless roadwork as the conditioning centrepiece. Inefficient for aerobic development in trained athletes, interferes with power development, and drives lower-limb injury.","type":"text"},{"text":"9. Treating conditioning as punishment. Every session must have a target adaptation. “Hard” is not an adaptation.","type":"text"},{"text":"10. No deloads, no off-season. Produces a slow decline that gets misdiagnosed as talent limitation.","type":"text"},{"text":"11. Neglecting sleep while spending money on supplements and recovery devices.","type":"text"},{"text":"12. No monitoring, no measurement. Without data you cannot distinguish under-recovery from lack of fitness, or progress from wishful thinking.","type":"text"},{"text":"13. Style imposed rather than developed. Beginners locked into a style before their attributes are known.","type":"text"},{"text":"14. Coach-dependency. Everything below is secondary.","type":"text"},{"text":"4.2.2 Neck training — the honest evidence","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Be clear about what is and is not established, because this is an area of considerable overstatement.","type":"text"},{"text":"What the evidence shows: - A systematic review with meta-analysis in team sports found very low-certainty evidence suggesting a small, non-significant relationship between greater neck strength and lower risk of sport-related concussion — pooled effects of r = 0.08–0.14 with substantial heterogeneity (Attwood et al., 2023, JOSPT) - A separate systematic review of S&C protocols for improving neck strength in collision sports found only three eligible papers; two showed significant improvements in isometric neck strength, and none reported any impact of neck strengthening on cervical spine injuries (Daly, Pearce & Ryan, 2021) - A further systematic review concluded that evidence remains inconclusive on the association between neck strength and concussion risk, though some studies reported positive trends - Individual studies report dose-response signals: for example, a reported ~13% reduction in concussion incidence per 10% increase in neck extension strength in 255 rugby players (adjusted IRR 0.87) - More consistently supported: greater cervical strength and, importantly, anticipatory muscle pre-activation appear to attenuate head kinematics — the linear and rotational accelerations that mediate injury. Short-latency anticipatory strength specifically has been reported to attenuate post-impact head kinematics - Recent systematic review plus Delphi consensus work has attempted to define best practice for neck training aimed at reducing head acceleration events (Fownes-Walpole et al., 2025)","type":"text"},{"text":"The practical position: train the neck. The mechanistic case is reasonable, the intervention is cheap and low-risk, the strength gains are reliable even where the injury-reduction evidence is not, and boxing is a sport whose entire premise is accelerating the head.","type":"text"},{"text":"But do not oversell it to yourself as protection that licenses more sparring. That is the failure mode. A stronger neck is not a helmet.","type":"text"},{"text":"4.2.3 The neck protocol","type":"subheading"},{"text":"3×/week, 8–10 min, integrated into warm-ups, permanently:","type":"text"},{"header":["Component","Prescription"],"rows":[{"Component":"Isometric holds — flexion, extension, both lateral flexions","Prescription":"3 × 10–15 s each, building to 3 × 30 s"},{"Component":"Manual-resistance or harness dynamic work","Prescription":"2 × 10 each plane, controlled tempo"},{"Component":"Band-resisted head rotation and anti-rotation","Prescription":"2 × 10 each direction"},{"Component":"Pre-activation drill","Prescription":"Brace the neck on a visual or auditory cue, then absorb a light controlled perturbation — a coach’s light push on the headgear, or a swinging bag tap. This trains the anticipatory response that appears most relevant to attenuating head kinematics"},{"Component":"Trap and scapular work","Prescription":"Integrated with shoulder work — the neck does not act alone"}],"type":"table"},{"text":"4.2.4 Other head-injury risk reduction","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Custom-fitted mouthguard, worn in all sparring. Mouthguards have significantly reduced oral injuries; the evidence for concussion reduction is weaker but the cost is nil","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Appropriate headgear during the training stages that call for it. Evidence indicates mandatory head guards plus modern thicker gloves significantly reduced knockouts and head injuries in boxing, though facial cuts increased when head guards were removed","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Appropriate glove weight — 16 oz for sparring, 18 oz for heavier boxers or size mismatches","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Careful partner matching on weight, experience and temperament","type":"bullet"},{"text":"A culture where reporting symptoms is normal. Grip/wrist: wrist circles, isometric grip 3 × 15 s, wrist extension band work × 15","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"4.5 Lower body and the permanent robustness circuit","order":5,"section":"LR-171","source":"LR-171 (The Long Road, Part 7, 4.5 Lower body and the permanent robustness circuit)","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"4.6.1 Recognition","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Suspect concussion after any blow to the head, face, neck, or body that transmits force to the head, if any of the following appear:","type":"text"},{"text":"Symptoms: headache, pressure in the head, dizziness, nausea, blurred or double vision, sensitivity to light or noise, feeling “slowed down,” “in a fog,” “not right,” difficulty concentrating or remembering, fatigue, irritability, emotional lability, sleep disturbance.","type":"text"},{"text":"Signs: loss of consciousness (in only a minority of concussions), blank or vacant look, lying motionless, slow to get up, unsteadiness, disorientation, confusion, inability to respond appropriately, facial injury with any of the above, seizure, tonic posturing.","type":"text"},{"text":"Immediate red flags requiring emergency evaluation: neck pain or tenderness, double vision, weakness or tingling in limbs, severe or increasing headache, seizure, loss of consciousness, deteriorating consciousness, vomiting, increasing restlessness or agitation.","type":"text"},{"text":"4.6.2 The immediate response","type":"subheading"},{"text":"1. Remove from activity immediately. “If in doubt, sit them out”","type":"text"},{"text":"2. No return to activity the same day","type":"text"},{"text":"3. Do not leave the athlete alone; monitor for deterioration","type":"text"},{"text":"4. Medical evaluation — a healthcare professional, not a coach’s judgment","type":"text"},{"text":"5. No alcohol, no driving, no unsupervised medication","type":"text"},{"text":"4.6.3 The graduated return-to-sport strategy","type":"subheading"},{"text":"The Amsterdam 2023 international consensus statement (Patricios et al., 2023, BJSM — the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport) provides the current framework, including an updated staged return-to-play protocol and updated assessment tools (SCAT6, Child SCAT6, SCOAT6, CRT6). The consensus organizes clinical management around a framework of “R”s — Recognize, Reduce, Remove, Re-evaluate, (Relative) Rest, Rehabilitate, Refer, Recover, Return-to-Learn/Return-to-Sport, Reconsider, Refine, and Retire — the last two being additions in the Amsterdam statement.","type":"text"},{"text":"The staged progression, adapted for boxing:","type":"text"},{"header":["Stage","Activity","Boxing content","Criteria to progress"],"rows":[{"Activity":"Symptom-limited activity","Boxing content":"Daily activities that do not exacerbate symptoms; light walking","Criteria to progress":"Tolerated without symptom exacerbation","Stage":"1"},{"Activity":"Light aerobic exercise","Boxing content":"Walking, stationary bike at low intensity","Criteria to progress":"24 h symptom-free at this level","Stage":"2"},{"Activity":"Sport-specific exercise, no head impact","Boxing content":"Shadow boxing, footwork, light bag work, running","Criteria to progress":"24 h symptom-free","Stage":"3"},{"Activity":"Non-contact training drills","Boxing content":"Full technical training, pads, bag work at normal intensity, conditioning, strength training","Criteria to progress":"24 h symptom-free","Stage":"4"},{"Activity":"Full contact practice — requires medical clearance","Boxing content":"Return to sparring, beginning at Stage 3–4 of the sparring continuum, not at the level you left","Criteria to progress":"Medical clearance obtained; no symptoms","Stage":"5"},{"Activity":"Return to competition","Boxing content":"Normal competitive activity","Criteria to progress":"All above cleared","Stage":"6"}],"type":"table"},{"text":"Rules: - Each stage requires at least 24 hours symptom-free before progressing - Any symptom recurrence returns the athlete to the previous stage - Stage 5 requires medical clearance, without exception - On return to sparring, drop back two stages of the sparring continuum and rebuild. Returning directly to hard sparring after a concussion is how second injuries happen - Most jurisdictions impose mandatory suspension periods after knockouts and technical knockouts — treat these as minimums, not targets, and extend generously","type":"text"},{"text":"4.6.4 Repeat concussions","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Escalating concern, and a mandatory specialist conversation, if any of these occur: - More than one concussion in a season - Progressively lower impact thresholds required to produce symptoms - Prolonged symptom duration (weeks rather than days) - Symptoms persisting between bouts - Declining neurocognitive test scores against personal baseline","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"4.6 Concussion management and return to sport","order":6,"section":"LR-172","source":"LR-172 (The Long Road, Part 7, 4.6 Concussion management and return to sport)","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"Criterion-based, not calendar-based. Progress only when: - Pain-free through full range of motion - Strength within 10% of the uninjured side (measured, not estimated) - Sport-specific capacity demonstrated at the required intensity - Movement quality restored on video","type":"text"},{"text":"Return to sparring last, after all other training is fully tolerated. And when you do, drop back two stages of the continuum.","type":"text"},{"text":"“It feels fine” is not a discharge criterion. 2026-11-09 (D-OQ195))"},{"blocks":[{"text":"Partner roles allow the room to create educationally useful live pictures without turning every round into an uncontrolled fight.","type":"text"},{"text":"Retreat Role","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Purpose","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Create a live picture where the athlete must own ground, maintain structure, and solve movement without chasing.","type":"text"},{"text":"Required Behaviors","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Give ground consistently enough that the athlete must pressure with feet and angle decisions.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Use defensive movement rather than constant trading.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Do not turn the round into a sprint.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Only score enough to keep the round honest.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Coach Watch Points","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Is the athlete cutting or simply following.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Does pressure remain calm.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Do exits still occur after scoring.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Is frustration changing decision timing.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Failure Signs","type":"subheading"},{"text":"The role athlete begins freelancing offensively instead of serving the movement picture.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"The target athlete starts reaching, running, or hand-chasing.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"The round shifts from controlled pursuit to random pursuit.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Downgrade Rules","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Reduce movement speed.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Shorten the round.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Return to floor work if the athlete cannot pressure without chasing.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Remove live offense from the retreat role temporarily if needed.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Pressure Role","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Purpose","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Create a live picture where the athlete must stay clean, organized, and feet-first under forward pressure.","type":"text"},{"text":"Required Behaviors","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Walk pressure in with intention rather than chaos.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Force the athlete to manage distance and exits.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Do not turn the pressure role into a brawl role.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Coach Watch Points","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Does the athlete panic or retain structure.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Can the athlete reset and re-angle without emotional retaliation.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Does the athlete use feet before hands.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Failure Signs","type":"subheading"},{"text":"The pressure role speeds up emotionally.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"The target athlete shells up without finding clean exits.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Rounds become about surviving intensity rather than solving the picture.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Downgrade Rules","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Reduce output but keep the pressure picture.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Use shorter rounds and earlier resets.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Move to controlled tactical live work if emotional speed replaces decision quality.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Chaos Role","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Purpose","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Create a controlled disorder picture so the athlete learns to identify the moment where structure is gone and must be re-established.","type":"text"},{"text":"Required Behaviors","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Disrupt rhythm, spacing, and predictability without abandoning coach control.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Use awkward entries, off-beat movement, or crowding within safe bounds.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Do not let chaos become random punishment.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Coach Watch Points","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Can the athlete recognize disorder early.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Does the athlete leave or reset instead of fighting harder inside the mess.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Can the athlete recover posture, breathing, and visual control.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Failure Signs","type":"subheading"},{"text":"The athlete starts enjoying the mess instead of solving it.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"The role athlete is creating danger instead of educational difficulty.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"The coach can no longer explain what the round is teaching.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Downgrade Rules","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Reduce the number of disruptions inside the round.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Shift from live chaos to staged disruption reps.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Stop immediately if the room begins practicing bad decisions as a norm.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Controlled Boxer Role","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Purpose","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Create a clean boxing picture where scoring quality, defensive discipline, and exchange clarity can be measured without exaggerated pressure or exaggerated retreat.","type":"text"},{"text":"Required Behaviors","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Box clean, at a controlled pace, with visible tactical structure.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Give the target athlete a live but understandable picture.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Keep the round useful for measuring execution.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Coach Watch Points","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Can the athlete score cleanly without extra noise.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Does the athlete respect exchange caps and exits.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Can the athlete identify winning and losing moments clearly.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Failure Signs","type":"subheading"},{"text":"The round becomes too polite to reveal anything useful.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"The round becomes unexpectedly competitive and leaves the controlled picture.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Athletes start changing the role out of pride.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Downgrade Rules","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Clarify the role and reduce the pace.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Stop and reassign if either athlete no longer serves the declared picture.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Use shorter, more focused rounds.","type":"bullet"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"Partner Role System","order":8,"section":"DOC-129 Sparring corrections begin multiplying.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Pressure Resolution Round","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Objective","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Test whether the athlete can solve forward pressure, retreat pressure, or ring pressure without abandoning structure.","type":"text"},{"text":"Standard Setup","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Choose one pressure picture only.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"State the desired solution before the round begins.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Use coaches to watch for the declared failure pattern.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Success Markers","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Athlete identifies and solves the pressure picture more than once.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Behavior target remains visible even after mistakes.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Round pace stays under coach control.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Stop Rules","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Pressure becomes emotional.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"The athlete starts inventing survival habits outside the system.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"The room can no longer tell what the round was for.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Edge Round","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Objective","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Train round openings and round closings where emotional acceleration often causes mistakes.","type":"text"},{"text":"Standard Setup","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Call out emphasis on first and last segment of the round.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Coach one edge problem only.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Do not overload the middle of the round with extra instructions.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Success Markers","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Athlete starts and finishes with discipline.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"No needless risk appears at the edges.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Cue remains usable at speed.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Stop Rules","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Athlete rushes opening exchanges.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Athlete hunts a late exchange out of emotion.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Coach loses the edge focus during the middle of the round.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Recovery Under Disruption Round","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Objective","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Test how quickly the athlete can return to system shape after contact, crowding, or error.","type":"text"},{"text":"Standard Setup","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Use a partner who can create repeated but controlled disruption triggers.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"State that the round is about recovery quality, not winning the exchanges.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Keep the coach focused on reset behavior.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Success Markers","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Reset is visible and fast.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Breathing, eyes, and feet recover before re-entry.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Athlete stops fighting the previous mistake.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Stop Rules","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Contact triggers emotional retaliation.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Athlete never gets back to shape.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Coach begins teaching too many layers instead of reinforcing It will take an hour and it determines whether the next decade is well spent. 2. Complete the medical screening in Part 2 §1 before your first session. Not after. Before. 3. Set up the monitoring system in Part 2 §5. It takes ten minutes and it is the difference between training and guessing. 4. Follow the 90-day start protocol in Part 8 §5. 5. Read Part 3 §1–2 (Phase 1) and Part 6 §1–3 (technical curriculum, early tiers). 6. Come back to Parts 4, 5 and the deeper sections as you reach them. Do not try to run Phase 3 programming in month four.","type":"text"},{"text":"If you already train and want to systematize: 1. Part 2 — test yourself honestly against the battery and the technical scorecard. Most people discover they are further from their self-assessment than expected. 2. Part 1 §2 (needs analysis) — check your current training against what the sport actually demands. The gaps are usually in buffering capacity, reactive strength, and sparring economy. 3. Part 6 §9 (sparring continuum) — audit your sparring. This is where most gyms are leaving skill on the table and taking damage for nothing. 4. Part 5 — rebuild your physical preparation around block sequencing.","type":"text"},{"text":"If you are a coach: Parts 1, 5, 6 and 8 carry the coaching content. Part 6 §2 (practice design and the constraint library) and Part 6 §9 (sparring) are the highest-leverage sections in the entire system.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"How to actually use this","order":1,"owner_rules":[{"changed_by":"Jason 2026-11-03 (D-PK82-8)","owner_source":"DOC-027 (Punxsy Master Source Manual v1, Athlete Intake and Assessment Source Manual v3, Intake Information Standard); DOC-027 (Punxsy Master Source Manual v1, Athlete Intake and Assessment Source Manual v3, Initial Placement Standard); DOC-027 (Punxsy Master Source Manual v1, Athlete Intake and Assessment Source Manual v3, Non Negotiable Assessment Rules)","owner_text":["Collect the minimum information needed to coach safely, place correctly, and avoid wasting early sessions with the wrong assumptions.","Classify the athlete first by readiness for A, B, or C drill demand inside the current room, not by ego status.","Placement should reflect movement quality, cue response, pressure response, and recovery ability.","Do not assign advanced live demands before baseline movement, cue response, and structural discipline are visible."],"rule":"A new member starts with the owner's intake (the minimum information needed to coach safely and place correctly) and an initial placement at A, B or C drill demand; no advanced live demand is assigned before baseline movement, cue response and structural discipline are visible (as the spine's T1 entry gate). LR-003's reading order stays as source text."}],"section":"LR-003","source":"LR-003 (The Long Road, front matter, How to actually use this)","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"If you read nothing else, read this.","type":"text"},{"text":"1. The timeline is long and the honest version matters. Sport-expertise research finds international-level athletes typically accumulate a decade or more in their sport, with reported practice requirements ranging from roughly 4,000 to well over 10,000 hours depending on the domain. Boxing sits at the high-skill end. Expect 4–7 years to national-level amateur, 6–10+ to international representation, 7–12 to professional contention. Starting age changes the ceiling, not the method.","type":"text"},{"text":"2. Skill is the ceiling; fitness is the floor. Conditioning does not make an unskilled boxer good. But poor conditioning stops a skilled boxer expressing skill in round 3, which is when bouts are decided.","type":"text"},{"text":"3. Head trauma is a finite lifetime budget and sparring is how you spend it. Instrumented mouthguard research has recorded a mean of roughly 42 head impacts per athlete in a single controlled two-minute sparring session, and one session of 3 × 3-min sparring produces measurable increases in corticomotor inhibition, altered motor unit recruitment, and reduced memory performance an hour later. Every round must buy something no cheaper round could buy.","type":"text"},{"text":"4. The sport is aerobically funded and alactically expressed. A 3 × 3-min amateur bout runs roughly 73% aerobic / 19% alactic / 8% glycolytic, at above 90% of maximum heart rate throughout, ending above 15 mmol·L⁻¹ blood lactate. Build the aerobic engine precisely. Build alactic power. Build buffering capacity as its own quality.","type":"text"},{"text":"5. Winners are more efficient, not busier. Notational analysis consistently shows winners landing a far higher proportion of punches (≈33% vs ≈23%) and missing into empty air far less (≈17% vs ≈27%) with similar total output; in elite women’s finals, winners threw fewer offensive actions but with markedly higher effectiveness ratios. Train accuracy, selection, and defense that counters — not volume.","type":"text"},{"text":"6. Punch power comes from the ground. Classic force-dynamometry work found leg drive contributed 38.6% of punch force in experienced boxers versus 16.5% in novices — the single clearest illustration in the sport that power is a coordination and lower-body strength problem, not an arm problem. Accordingly: train lower-body maximal and explosive strength; train upper-body explosive strength. Upper-body maximal strength does not distinguish hard from soft punchers at elite level.","type":"text"},{"text":"7. Practice must be representative. Skills built in decontextualized isolation transfer badly. Constrained live formats do most of the learning at a fraction of hard sparring’s cost.","type":"text"},{"text":"8. Periodize, sequence, deload. Concentrated blocks with defined targets, exploiting residual training effects. Not everything at moderate intensity forever.","type":"text"},{"text":"9. Measure, or you are guessing. Session-RPE load, readiness, body mass, sparring rounds, head-impact exposure, a countermovement jump, and a technical scorecard. Ten minutes a week.","type":"text"},{"text":"10. The pursuit has to be worth it whether or not the top tier arrives. Most people who start with elite ambitions do not reach the elite. That is a reason to train carefully, not carelessly. A boxer who reaches national amateur level with an intact brain, a body that still works at fifty, and a decade of hard-won skill has had an excellent career.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"The one-page summary","order":2,"section":"LR-004","source":"LR-004 (The Long Road, front matter, The one-page summary)","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57)"},{"backbone_differences":[{"backbone":"No current physical on file: no USA Boxing-style athlete physical (Masters form for Masters) within 12 months.","backbone_source":"data/spine/spine.json app_notes 'no_current_physical' (Jason 2026-10-24, RULES s9 'Physicals'; notes only, never blocks)","card":"B9-PK02-1","label":"decided at final review (Jason 2026-11-08, D-PK83-1-FR, A; ACTIONS A-60): Jason's physicals rule (RULES s9) governs, unchanged; the Long Road's fuller screen is shown as information","long_road":"Obtain medical clearance before beginning.","reading":"PPBF asks for one physical within 12 months for sparring (a reminder, never a block); for anyone planning to compete, the Long Road recommends a fuller screen (listed in the track 'Medical Screening and Clearance', LR-025); discuss it with your physician. Governing Principles, In Depth","groups":[{"blocks":[{"text":"The Balyi Long-Term Athlete Development model (Balyi & Hamilton, 2004; Balyi, Way & Higgs, 2013) has been enormously influential; many national governing bodies adopted it. Its stage logic — Active Start, FUNdamentals, Learn to Train, Train to Train, Train to Compete, Train to Win, Active for Life — remains a useful organizing frame for thinking about development as a multi-year progression rather than a series of seasons.","type":"text"},{"text":"What has been criticized, and correctly: a group of UK researchers including Lloyd and Oliver published a critical review (Ford et al., 2011, J Sports Sci) identifying that the model is one-dimensional (physiological only, ignoring psychological, social and skill dimensions); that there is a lack of empirical evidence for its central “windows of opportunity” for trainability; that the data underpinning it rest on questionable assumptions and methods; and that it is generic rather than individualized.","type":"text"},{"text":"What replaced it on the physical side: the Youth Physical Development model (Lloyd & Oliver, 2012) and the NSCA position statement on long-term athletic development (Lloyd et al., 2016). Their central conclusion is directly relevant to an adult beginner: most, if not all, components of fitness are trainable throughout development. There is no window you have missed.","type":"text"},{"text":"Translation for this system:","type":"text"},{"text":"1. Train everything; emphasize sequentially. There is no need to wait for a window. There is every need to prioritize, because attention, recovery and time are finite.","type":"text"},{"text":"2. Training age governs progression, not chronological age. A 32-year-old former collegiate athlete with three months of boxing is a boxing beginner. Their strength training can progress fast; their sparring cannot.","type":"text"},{"text":"3. Technical competency gates load. Never add load, intensity, complexity or contact to a movement or situation the athlete cannot execute competently at a lower level. This applies identically to a barbell squat and to a sparring round.","type":"text"},{"text":"4. Multi-dimensional development or nothing. Physical, technical, tactical, psychological, and lifestyle domains all progress or the athlete stalls. The most common stall in adult boxers is physical progress without tactical or psychological progress.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"3.1 Long-term athlete development — what to take and what to discard","order":1,"owner_rules":[{"changed_by":"Jason 2026-11-03 (D-PK82-4)","owner_source":"DOC-027 (Punxsy Master Source Manual v1, Scaling and Progression Source Manual v3, Primary Progression Principle); DOC-027 (Punxsy Master Source Manual v1, Scaling and Progression Source Manual v3, Readiness Gates for Progression)","owner_text":["Athletes should progress by proving decision quality, structure, and composure under the current demand level before moving to a harder one.","The athlete can repeat the target behavior with one cue only.","The athlete can recover after one mistake without forgetting the lesson.","The athlete can maintain balance, breathing, and visual control during the drill.","The athlete can finish the rep without creating a new avoidable problem.","The athlete is not using speed to hide confusion."],"rule":"An athlete moves to a higher demand (load, intensity, complexity or sparring stage) when the owner's readiness gates are visible: the target behaviour with one cue only; recovery after one mistake without losing the lesson; balance, breathing and visual control; a finished rep without a new avoidable problem; no speed hiding confusion. It is never a default activity, a fitness session, a test of character, or a way to fill time.","type":"text"},{"text":"3.2.1 The reasoning","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Sparring is simultaneously the highest-value and highest-cost training method in boxing. High value because it is the only method containing the full information of competition: a live, adaptive, resisting opponent with intent to hit you. High cost because of §2.4.2.","type":"text"},{"text":"Almost every other training decision in boxing has a cost that is recoverable. Overdo the running and you get sore. Overdo the strength work and you get tired. Overdo the sparring and you spend something you cannot get back.","type":"text"},{"text":"3.2.2 The operating rules","type":"subheading"},{"text":"1. Every round answers a question. Before a round starts, the boxer states the objective. “This round I’m working on exiting at an angle after the rear hand.” A round with no stated objective is unpaid trauma.","type":"text"},{"text":"2. Hard sparring is a peaking and specific-preparation tool, not a development tool. Skills are built in constrained, live-but-controlled formats. Hard sparring tests them, and develops the specific psychological and metabolic tolerances of competition. Confusing these two is the single most common and most damaging error in boxing.","type":"text"},{"text":"3. Volume of hard sparring is inversely related to career length. Gyms producing long careers characteristically spar hard rarely and under tight supervision. Gyms running 100+ hard rounds per camp produce boxers who peak early and decline neurologically.","type":"text"},{"text":"4. Never spar within 24–48 hours of a session where cognitive or neuromuscular quality matters — new technical acquisition, maximal strength, maximal velocity work.","type":"text"},{"text":"5. Track it like sets and reps. Sparring rounds per week, stage, and a subjective head-impact score belong in the log. What isn’t measured drifts upward.","type":"text"},{"text":"6. The lower stages do most of the work. If a skill can be developed at Stage 4 (constrained live) or Stage 6 (situational), developing it at Stage 7 (hard) is a waste of neurological budget.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"3.2 The sparring economy — the central organizing principle","order":2,"owner_rules":[{"changed_by":"Jason 2026-11-03 (D-PK82-3)","owner_source":"DOC-027 (Punxsy Master Source Manual v1, Core Source Manual v3, Sparring Standard)","owner_text":["Sparring exists to test decisions, not ego.","Every round must have a role, a purpose, and a coaching focus.","If chaos rises above the educational value of the round, intensity is reduced or the round is stopped."],"rule":"Every sparring round has a role, a purpose and a coaching focus, with the boxer's stated objective as part of it; when chaos rises above the round's educational value, intensity is reduced or the round is stopped. LR-019's operating rules stay as source text and starting defaults."}],"section":"LR-019","source":"LR-019 (The Long Road, Part 1, 3.2 The sparring economy — the central organizing principle)","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"3.3.1 Why the traditional model under-delivers","type":"subheading"},{"text":"The traditional model is: demonstrate technique → drill technique in isolation → apply technique in sparring. This works reasonably for closed skills. It under-delivers for open skills because it separates the movement from the information that should trigger and shape it. A boxer who has drilled 10,000 slips against a coach’s predictable jab has learned to slip on a cue that does not exist in a fight.","type":"text"},{"text":"3.3.2 The ecological / constraints-led alternative","type":"subheading"},{"text":"The theoretical basis is that skill emerges from the interaction of three sets of constraints (Newell, 1986): - Organismic — the athlete’s height, reach, strength, fatigue state, anxiety, prior experience - Environmental — the ring, the gloves, the crowd, the referee, the score - Task — the rules, the objective, the equipment","type":"text"},{"text":"Coaches cannot install technique. They can design environments in which the desired behavior is the most attractive available solution, and let the athlete find it. This has three practical consequences:","type":"text"},{"text":"Representative learning design (Pinder et al., 2011): practice must contain the same information sources as competition. If the information is different, the skill learned is different.","type":"text"},{"text":"Functional variability: the goal is not one repeatable movement but an adaptable solution space. Expect — and want — variability from repetition to repetition, because the conditions vary. “Repetition without repetition”: same intention, different execution.","type":"text"},{"text":"Constraint manipulation as the primary coaching tool: rather than instructing “keep your hands up,” design a task in which dropping the hands loses the round. The behavior then emerges and is owned by the athlete, rather than being complied with and abandoned under pressure.","type":"text"},{"text":"There is also evidence that the affective dimension matters. Work with internationally competitive taekwondo athletes found that adding competition constraints — a visible scoreboard with time and score — changed measurable behavior including attack rate and preferred interpersonal distance (Maloney et al., 2018), and the broader finding is that training without the emotional information of competition does not prepare athletes for competition. Composure has to be practiced with something at stake.","type":"text"},{"text":"3.3.3 Progressive coupling — the ladder every skill climbs","type":"subheading"},{"header":["Rung","Format","What it develops","Head-impact cost"],"rows":[{"Format":"Shadow / mirror","Head-impact cost":"Zero","Rung":"1","What it develops":"Pattern formation, self-perception, volume without cost"},{"Format":"Air work with external-focus cues + video","Head-impact cost":"Zero","Rung":"2","What it develops":"Mechanics with feedback"},{"Format":"Bag / pads, predictable feed","Head-impact cost":"Zero","Rung":"3","What it develops":"Force production, rhythm, conditioning"},{"Format":"Pads with unpredictable feed","Head-impact cost":"Zero","Rung":"4","What it develops":"Perception-action coupling begins"},{"Format":"Cooperative partner, low speed, defined roles","Head-impact cost":"Near zero","Rung":"5","What it develops":"Live information, safe"},{"Format":"Constrained live (one hand, touch only, body only, defense only)","Head-impact cost":"Low","Rung":"6","What it develops":"Skill emerges under real pressure"},{"Format":"Open live at controlled intensity","Head-impact cost":"Moderate","Rung":"7","What it develops":"Integration"},{"Format":"Competition-representative","Head-impact cost":"High","Rung":"8","What it develops":"Expression under full demand"}],"type":"table"},{"text":"Critically: a boxer sits at different rungs for different skills simultaneously. They may be at rung 7 for the jab and rung 4 for the check hook. Programming a whole session at one rung wastes the session.","type":"text"},{"text":"Farrow and Robertson’s (2017) skill acquisition periodization framework adds a useful layer: skill work should itself be periodized across a season according to whether the current goal is acquisition (learning something new — needs low pressure, high feedback, fresh athlete), refinement (improving something known — needs variability), or expression under pressure (needs representativeness and consequence). Trying to acquire new skills in fight week is a category error.","type":"text"},{"text":"3.3.4 Feedback and cueing","type":"subheading"},{"text":"External focus beats internal focus for motor performance and learning in a large body of motor-learning research. Practically: - Internal cue (worse): “rotate your hip, then extend your arm, keep your elbow in” - External cue (better): “land it so your shoulder finishes where his shoulder was” - External cue (better): “punch through the pad, not to it”","type":"text"},{"text":"Use less feedback than feels natural. Constant coaching creates dependency on the coach’s voice, which is absent in the ring. Bandwidth feedback (only when performance falls outside a range) and delayed feedback (after a set of reps, not every rep) produce better retention than continuous feedback, even though continuous feedback produces better performance during practice. Beyond molecular signalling, there are simpler explanations: residual fatigue, glycogen depletion, and muscle damage degrade the quality of the subsequent session.","type":"text"},{"text":"Since Hickson’s original 1980 observation, the literature has settled into something like this: - Wilson et al.’s (2012) meta-analysis of 21 studies found small-to-moderate impairment of lower-body strength (SMD ≈ −0.3) and power (−0.3 to −0.4) when aerobic work was added to resistance training, with hypertrophy less affected - Interference scales with weekly aerobic volume and with proximity to the resistance session - Running produces greater interference than cycling, likely via eccentric loading and muscle damage - HIIT appears to interfere less than moderate-intensity continuous work - Intra-session sequence effects are small; a meta-analysis found support for resistance-before-endurance specifically for lower-body dynamic strength outcomes, and little else - Separating sessions by at least ~6 hours appears to minimize acute interference - Higher-level athletes are more susceptible than novices, particularly for speed and power qualities","type":"text"},{"text":"3.4.2 The rules this produces","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Separation: where possible, ≥6 hours between conflicting sessions, or different days.","type":"text"},{"text":"Sequence within a session: resistance before endurance, unless the specific goal is technique-under-fatigue.","type":"text"},{"text":"Modality selection: during maximal strength and power blocks, shift conditioning to cycle, rower, or curved treadmill and reduce running volume. athletes so challenge stays productive and the athlete can still absorb the main lesson.","type":"text"},{"text":"Standards","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Give one focus and one cue that can be used immediately.","type":"text"},{"text":"Use tasks that are simple enough to repeat but challenging enough to require attention.","type":"text"},{"text":"Expect correction, but do not overload the athlete with adult-level explanation density.","type":"text"},{"text":"Protect progress by asking for clean repetitions before asking for high-speed variability.","type":"text"},{"text":"Use structure attention loss is laziness when instruction load was too high.","type":"text"},{"text":"Corrections and Responses","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Reduce words before reducing standards.","type":"text"},{"text":"Use demonstration and simple language together.","type":"text"},{"text":"Return to the main rule when the athlete gets cognitively lost.","type":"text"},{"text":"Keep the demand high enough to build growth but low enough to remain coachable.","type":"text"},{"text":"Use Case","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Use with all developing performance.","type":"text"},{"text":"Standards","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Early repetitions should be clean enough that the athlete can identify the target pattern.","type":"text"},{"text":"Variability should be added once the target pattern exists, not before.","type":"text"},{"text":"The athlete should experience both clear repetition and controlled problem solving.","type":"text"},{"text":"Motor learning is strongest when the athlete gets enough repetition to stabilize the behavior and enough variation to retain it under different pictures.","type":"text"},{"text":"Feedback should guide the next rep, not flood the athlete with analysis.","type":"text"},{"text":"Watch Points","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Does the athlete know what the successful rep felt like.","type":"text"},{"text":"Is variability helping transfer or only creating confusion.","type":"text"},{"text":"Is the coach correcting the first break in the chain or only the final visible mistake.","type":"text"},{"text":"Are repetitions staying clean enough to teach the intended lesson.","type":"text"},{"text":"Common Errors","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Adding live variability before the athlete has a stable base rep.","type":"text"},{"text":"Using too much blocked repetition for too long and then being surprised by poor transfer.","type":"text"},{"text":"Correcting every detail and burying the main motor target.","type":"text"},{"text":"Corrections and Responses","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Start with a stable picture, then add one useful variation at a time.","type":"text"},{"text":"Preserve one clear rep image the athlete can return to.","type":"text"},{"text":"If transfer is failing, return briefly to a cleaner pattern before rebuilding variation.","type":"text"},{"text":"Use Case","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Use for drill design, weekly progression, and all stages of technical organized so the lesson survives practice instead of being lost in noise.","type":"text"},{"text":"Standards","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Use short cues that target the action the athlete must perform now.","type":"text"},{"text":"Cues should help attention move outward toward task-relevant information whenever possible.","type":"text"},{"text":"The room should protect attention by reducing unnecessary waiting, over-talking, and side instruction.","type":"text"},{"text":"One cue is stronger than many competing reminders.","type":"text"},{"text":"Watch Points","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Does the athlete act faster and cleaner after the cue, or only look more confused.","type":"text"},{"text":"Are athletes waiting too long and losing focus between reps.","type":"text"},{"text":"Is the cue attached to the correct part of the action chain.","type":"text"},{"text":"Common Errors","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Cue stacking.","type":"text"},{"text":"Using a different phrase every rep for the same problem.","type":"text"},{"text":"Talking through the action rather than allowing the athlete to act.","type":"text"},{"text":"Corrections and Responses","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Keep cues stable across sessions when the target remains the same.","type":"text"},{"text":"Shorten the gap between explanation and action.","type":"text"},{"text":"If attention is drifting, simplify the room before raising your voice.","type":"text"},{"text":"Use Case","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Use in every youth session and especially in mixed-level rooms where attention can fragment quickly.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"Attention and Cue Design the lesson into therapy or ignoring emotional reality.","type":"text"},{"text":"Standards","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Emotional regulation is taught through drill design, correction structure, resets, and coach tone.","type":"text"},{"text":"The athlete should repeatedly experience that mistakes are recoverable and that the next correct action matters more than emotional reaction.","type":"text"},{"text":"Reset behavior should be coached as a skill, not only demanded as discipline.","type":"text"},{"text":"The room should make calm look strong and usable.","type":"text"},{"text":"Watch Points","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Does the athlete speed up after mistakes.","type":"text"},{"text":"Does the athlete lose decision quality when frustrated.","type":"text"},{"text":"Can the athlete return to the cue after a bad rep or a hard round.","type":"text"},{"text":"Is the coach tone calming or escalating the emotional state.","type":"text"},{"text":"Common Errors","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Using anger to teach control.","type":"text"},{"text":"Ignoring the emotional side of breakdowns and calling everything technical.","type":"text"},{"text":"Allowing young athletes to sit in frustration without giving them a recovery process.","type":"text"},{"text":"Corrections and Responses","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Use visible reset rules such as breathe, stance, eyes, then act.","type":"text"},{"text":"Reinforce quick recovery rather than only error-free performance.","type":"text"},{"text":"If the athlete is emotionally flooded, reduce complexity and restore one clean success rep.","type":"text"},{"text":"Use Case","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Use after contact, after errors, during sparring, and during high-frustration learning phases.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"Emotional Regulation Teaching overreacting or lowering standards too far.","type":"text"},{"text":"Standards","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Growth phases can temporarily disturb coordination, rhythm, and timing.","type":"text"},{"text":"The coach should expect periods where the athlete looks less smooth while still being highly trainable.","type":"text"},{"text":"Standards remain, but the path back to clean movement may require more stability, slower reps, and clearer cues for a period.","type":"text"},{"text":"The system should adapt demand without changing core identity.","type":"text"},{"text":"Watch Points","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Has the athlete’s usual timing shifted recently.","type":"text"},{"text":"Do errors look like confusion, growth-related simplifying the picture.","type":"text"},{"text":"Corrections and Responses","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Reduce speed before reducing standards.","type":"text"},{"text":"Use cleaner rep pictures for One cue may lead to one of two permitted responses.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Level three is moving read. The cue appears in motion and the athlete must stay organized while identifying it.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Level four is disrupted read. decision-relevant.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Watch Points","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Does the athlete respond to the important cue or to the loudest cue.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Is the athlete once.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Common Errors","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Training perception with too many simultaneous visual demands early.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Rewarding reactions to fake cues because they look quick.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Teaching athletes to scan everything instead of attending to what matters most.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Corrections and Responses","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Use one signal family at a time in early stages.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Coach athletes to name the real cue after the rep.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"If and small corrections to solve the picture before late emergency reactions are needed.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"The athlete should be trained to see the moment before the breakdown, not only the
