Points","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Does the athlete act before the exchange fully collapses.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Can the athlete identify the first shift that signaled the next problem.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Does earlier seeing produce smaller more efficient solutions.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Common Errors","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Only reacting after the punch or crowding is already fully there.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Calling dramatic late saves good defense when early recognition would have prevented the need.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Teaching reaction without teaching anticipation.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Corrections and Responses","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Use slow-to-moderate staged pictures and freeze at the earliest useful moment.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Coach pre-cues such as line opening, shoulder commitment, or crowding approach rather than only final impact moments.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"If the athlete is always late, slow the rep and expand the early window first.","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Use Case","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Use in defense, reset, countering, and crowding-management details: {"chapter_heading":"5. Distance Management — The Full Curriculum","groups":[{"blocks":[{"text":"Look again at the notational finding: winners’ air-punch rate is ~17%; losers’ is ~27%. An air punch is, almost always, a punch thrown from outside the range at which it could land. That is not a punching problem. It is a distance problem.","type":"text"},{"text":"Distance management also determines: whether you get hit, whether your power transfers, whether you can counter, and whether the opponent can execute their plan at all.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"5.1 Why this is the highest-leverage under-taught skill","order":1,"section":"LR-124","source":"LR-124 (The Long Road, Part 6, 5.1 Why this is the highest-leverage under-taught skill)","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"Stage 1 — Know your own ranges (measure them)","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Physically measure and mark: - The distance at which your jab lands at full extension without over-reaching - The distance at which your rear hand lands - The distance at which your lead hook lands - The distance at which your uppercut lands","type":"text"},{"text":"Mark these on the floor with tape. Drill from each, so the feel of each range becomes recognizable without looking. Most boxers have never done this and could not tell you their own rear-hand range within 15 cm.","type":"text"},{"text":"Stage 2 — Know their ranges","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Repeat the measurement against partners of different heights and reaches. Learn to estimate an opponent’s range from their build, and to verify it in the first thirty seconds of a bout — which is one of the real purposes of the range-finding jab.","type":"text"},{"text":"Stage 3 — The gap","type":"subheading"},{"text":"The distance where your shots land and theirs do not. Often 10–15 cm.","type":"text"},{"text":"Drill: partner throws at a fixed rhythm; the boxer’s only job is to remain in their own scoring range and outside the partner’s. No punching. 4 × 2 min. details: {"chapter_heading":"2. Strength and Power Programming","groups":[{"blocks":[{"text":"Three findings drive everything in this section.","type":"text"},{"text":"Finding 1: punch force comes from the ground, and increasingly so with expertise. Filimonov’s force-dynamometry work found leg drive contributing ~38.6% of punch force in experienced boxers, ~32.2% in intermediate, and ~16.5% in novices, with trunk rotation ~37.4% and arm extension ~24.1% in advanced boxers. Boxers classified as knockout artists showed the highest leg contribution.","type":"text"},{"text":"Finding 2: the strength qualities that matter are asymmetric between upper and lower body. Beattie and Ruddock’s (2022) review found that lower-body maximal strength and lower-body explosive strength are both largely associated with punch impact force in elite amateurs, and that elite amateurs who punch hard have greater lower-body maximal and explosive strength than elite amateurs who punch softly. Upper-body maximal strength showed no such association and did not differentiate hard from soft punchers; only upper-body explosive strength did. Their recommendation: emphasize both maximal and explosive strength in the legs, with an explosive-strength focus only in the upper body.","type":"text"},{"text":"Finding 3: the sport under-uses maximal strength training for cultural reasons. Beattie and Ruddock’s (2025) survey of boxing practitioners found that 84% acknowledged maximal strength training improves punching power, yet it was the least programmed modality, while punch-specific and reactive-strength training were the most programmed (93%), and respondents identified a persistent fear within boxing that maximum-strength training is harmful to boxers.","type":"text"},{"text":"There is one important caveat to Finding 2, raised in critical commentary: the analyses did not fully adjust for body mass, so part of the association between strength and punch force reflects bigger fighters being both stronger and harder-hitting. The practical correction is to prioritize strength relative to body mass and avoid unnecessary mass gain — which is what a weight-category sport requires anyway.","type":"text"},{"text":"And one more: recent work on lower-limb kinetics found that after a fatiguing lower-body circuit, punch force fell significantly across all punch types, with the largest drops in the cross and lead hook, and larger drops in each individual’s weakest punches than their strongest. Lower-body strength and endurance are therefore not only power qualities — they are round-3 power-retention qualities.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"2.1 The evidence base, restated as programming decisions","order":1,"section":"LR-090","source":"LR-090 (The Long Road, Part 5, 2.1 The evidence base, restated as programming decisions)","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"2.2.1 Lower-body maximal strength","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Trap-bar deadlift — usually the best first choice for a boxer. - Why: high load tolerance, short learning curve, more upright torso than a straight-bar deadlift so less lumbar shear, and it loads the hip and knee extensors that drive the punch - Setup: mid-foot under the handles, shins near the bar, hips higher than a squat but lower than a stiff-leg, chest up, lats engaged, neutral spine - Execution: push the floor away rather than pulling the bar up; hips and shoulders rise together; finish tall without hyperextending - Common faults: hips shooting up first (load too heavy or hamstring stiffness), rounding at the start (set the lats before pulling), bar drifting forward (weight in the mid-foot, not the toes) - Boxing relevance: trains the triple-extension pattern underlying leg drive - Prescription: 4–5 × 3–5 @ 80–88%","type":"text"},{"text":"Back squat - Why: the highest-loading knee-and-hip extension pattern; strong evidence base for developing lower-body maximal strength - Setup: bar in the high or low position (consistency matters more than which), feet at a width allowing full depth without lumbar flexion, toes slightly out - Execution: brace, break at the hips and knees together, descend to at least parallel with a neutral spine, drive up with the chest staying up - Common faults: knees collapsing inward (glute and adductor weakness, or ankle restriction), butt tucking at depth (ankle dorsiflexion or hip mobility — retest the screen), forward lean (thoracic stiffness or weak trunk) - Caution for boxers: axial loading during high-sparring weeks can aggravate a cervical spine that is already taking impact. Substitute a trap-bar deadlift, belt squat, or safety-bar squat in those weeks","type":"text"},{"text":"Front squat — more upright, less axial compression, more quadriceps and trunk demand. Useful alternative; the limiting factor is usually wrist and thoracic mobility.","type":"text"},{"text":"Rear-foot-elevated split squat — the highest-value single-leg exercise for a boxer. - Why: boxing is a staggered-stance sport. Bilateral strength does not automatically transfer to a split stance. This exercise trains the exact position from which you punch - Setup: rear foot on a bench roughly knee height, front foot far enough forward that the front shin stays near-vertical at the bottom, torso upright - Execution: descend under control until the rear knee approaches the floor, drive through the whole front foot - Coaching cue: “own the bottom position” — pause for a beat to eliminate bouncing - Prescription: 3 × 6–8/side @ RPE 7–8","type":"text"},{"text":"Romanian deadlift — posterior chain, hamstring length under load, hip hinge pattern. - Execution: hips back, minimal knee bend, bar tracing the thighs, descend until hamstring tension limits range with a neutral spine, drive hips forward - Common fault: turning it into a squat or a back extension","type":"text"},{"text":"Nordic hamstring curl — the best available eccentric hamstring exercise, with a strong injury-prevention evidence base in sports involving sprinting. - Prescription: 3 × 5, controlled to the point of failure of the eccentric, catching with the hands - Warning: extremely soreness-producing on first exposure. Start with 2 × 3 partial-range reps","type":"text"},{"text":"Hip thrust — glute-dominant hip extension with minimal spinal loading. Useful during high-sparring weeks.","type":"text"},{"text":"Belt squat / hack squat / safety-bar squat — load the legs with reduced axial or shoulder demand. Genuinely useful in a sport where the cervical spine and shoulders are already stressed.","type":"text"},{"text":"2.2.2 Lower-body explosive strength and power","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Jump squat (bodyweight or loaded 20–40% 1RM) - Execution: rapid countermovement, maximal jump, soft landing, reset between reps - Prescription: 4–6 × 3 with full recovery. Maximum intent every rep. If you are not trying to jump as high as possible, this exercise does nothing - Load selection: lighter loads (20–30%) bias velocity; heavier (30–40%) bias force. Use both across a block","type":"text"},{"text":"Olympic lift derivatives — hang clean, clean pull, high pull, snatch pull - Why: among the highest measured power outputs of any resistance exercise, and they train the rapid triple extension that underlies leg drive - The honest caveat: the learning cost is real. A boxer’s training time is limited and technique acquisition can consume months. Only use these with competent coaching. The pulls (clean pull, high pull, snatch pull) capture most of the benefit with a fraction of the learning cost, because you do not have to catch the bar - Prescription: 4–5 × 3 @ 70–85%","type":"text"},{"text":"Trap-bar jump — an excellent compromise: loaded triple extension with almost no learning curve. 4 × 3 @ 20–30% of trap-bar deadlift 1RM.","type":"text"},{"text":"Broad jump, vertical jump, box jump — foundational, teach landing, quantifiable. - Box jump caution: box height measures how well you tuck your knees, not how high you jump. Use a moderate box and focus on takeoff speed and landing quality. Step down; do not jump down","type":"text"},{"text":"Hurdle hops, pogo hops, ankle stiffness work — fast plyometrics for reactive strength.","type":"text"},{"text":"Depth jumps and drop jumps — the highest-intensity plyometric and the direct intervention for the boxers’ eccentric-utilization deficit. - Progression: 20 cm box → 30 cm → 40 cm, advancing only when contact time stays short and height stays high - Instruction: “off the ground as fast as possible, as high as possible” - Prescription: 3–5 × 3–5 with full recovery. Very low volume. Very high quality. Stop at the first sign of degradation","type":"text"},{"text":"Sled pushes and short sprints — horizontal force production, relevant to closing distance.","type":"text"},{"text":"2.2.3 Upper-body explosive strength — the priority","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Medicine ball single-arm “punch” throw — the cornerstone exercise, and the best field test. - Setup: seated (back against a wall to remove legs, or on a bench to allow trunk) or standing (full kinetic chain) - Execution: punching action, maximum velocity, full follow-through - Prescription: 4–6 × 3–5 per arm, full recovery, 3–4 kg ball - Progress by: distance thrown at fixed mass, not by increasing mass indefinitely. Heavy medicine balls turn a power exercise into a strength exercise and lose the point","type":"text"},{"text":"Medicine ball rotational throw — trunk rotational power, the middle link of the kinetic chain. Side-on to a wall, 4 × 4/side.","type":"text"},{"text":"Medicine ball overhead slam and chest pass — general upper-body ballistic power, easy to load and progress.","type":"text"},{"text":"Ballistic bench press throw — in a rack with safety pins, on a Smith machine, or with a landmine setup. 4 × 3 @ 30–45% 1RM, maximum velocity, released at the top where equipment allows.","type":"text"},{"text":"Plyometric push-ups, clap push-ups, drop push-ups — upper-body reactive strength. - Progression: explosive push-up (hands leave floor) → clap → drop from a low box → depth push-up - 3–4 × 3–5, full recovery","type":"text"},{"text":"Landmine rotational press and landmine punch press — a punching pattern under load, with the rotational component preserved. 3 × 6/side, explosive intent.","type":"text"},{"text":"Band-resisted punching — used correctly this is a power exercise: 3–4 sets of 6–10 maximal punches per side with full recovery, resistance light enough that punch velocity is barely reduced. Used incorrectly — rounds of resisted punching for conditioning — it degrades punch mechanics and loads the shoulder in a compromised position for hundreds of reps.","type":"text"},{"text":"2.2.4 Upper-body strength — supporting, moderate priority","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Weighted chin-up and pull-up — the primary upper-body strength exercise for a boxer. Trains the lats (which contribute to punch retraction and trunk connection), builds relative strength, and supports shoulder health through balanced volume. - 4 × 3–6 with added mass, or bodyweight progressions","type":"text"},{"text":"Barbell row, dumbbell row, single-arm row — horizontal pulling volume. Boxers need more pulling than pushing: minimum 1:1, preferably 2:1 pull-to-push, because punching volume already loads the anterior shoulder heavily.","type":"text"},{"text":"Overhead press (standing) — trains the trunk-to-shoulder force transmission link and maintains overhead capacity. Only if overhead range of motion is adequate; force it and you will find a shoulder impingement.","type":"text"},{"text":"Bench press or floor press — track it as a general strength marker, keep the volume moderate, and do not let it dominate. It is not associated with punch impact force. Floor press is often preferable for boxers: less shoulder extension at the bottom, less anterior capsule stress.","type":"text"},{"text":"Face pulls, external rotation at multiple angles, prone Y/T/W, serratus work — non-negotiable shoulder health volume, 3×/week.","type":"text"},{"text":"2.2.5 Trunk and force transmission","type":"subheading"},{"text":"The trunk’s job in boxing is transmitting force from the legs to the arms without leaking, and resisting the rotation the opponent’s shots impose. Note that trunk rotation contributes ~37% of punch force in advanced boxers — this is not “core work for abs,” it is a primary force contributor.","type":"text"},{"header":["Exercise","Purpose","Prescription"],"rows":[{"Exercise":"Pallof press and variants","Prescription":"3 × 10/side","Purpose":"Anti-rotation — resisting the rotation you don’t want"},{"Exercise":"Cable/band rotational chop at speed","Prescription":"3 × 8/side, fast","Purpose":"Rotational power production"},{"Exercise":"Landmine rotation","Prescription":"3 × 8/side","Purpose":"Loaded rotation through range"},{"Exercise":"Rotational deceleration (catch and stop a rotational throw)","Prescription":"3 × 6/side","Purpose":"The ability to stop rotation — protects the spine and allows the next punch"},{"Exercise":"Dead bug, bird dog","Prescription":"2–3 × 8/side","Purpose":"Trunk stability with limb movement"},{"Exercise":"Side plank variants","Prescription":"2 × 30–45 s/side","Purpose":"Lateral trunk endurance"},{"Exercise":"Loaded carries (farmer’s, suitcase, front-rack)","Prescription":"3 × 30–40 m","Purpose":"Integrated trunk, grip, posture under load"},{"Exercise":"Hanging leg raise / ab wheel","Prescription":"3 × 8–12","Purpose":"Anterior chain strength"}],"type":"table"},{"text":"What to avoid: high-volume crunches and sit-ups. Repeated lumbar flexion under load, thousands of reps, in a sport that already loads the spine rotationally. Little benefit, real cost.","type":"text"},{"text":"2.2.6 Neck training","type":"subheading"},{"text":"The rationale, the evidence, and the honest limits are in Part 7 §4.2. The protocol:","type":"text"},{"header":["Exercise","Prescription"],"rows":[{"Exercise":"Isometric holds — flexion, extension, both lateral flexions","Prescription":"3 × 10–15 s each, building to 3 × 30 s"},{"Exercise":"Manual resistance or harness dynamic work — all planes","Prescription":"2 × 10 each, controlled tempo"},{"Exercise":"Band-resisted head rotation and anti-rotation","Prescription":"2 × 10 each direction"},{"Exercise":"Pre-activation drill — brace on a cue, absorb a light controlled perturbation","Prescription":"2 × 5 per cue type"},{"Exercise":"Trap and scapular work (upper trap shrugs, scapular retraction)","Prescription":"Integrated with shoulder work"}],"type":"table"},{"text":"Frequency: 3×/week minimum, integrated into warm-ups. Forever. The evidence is laid out in Part 1 §2.4.2; the summary:","type":"text"},{"text":"Instrumented mouthguards recorded ~42 head impacts per male athlete in a single controlled two-minute sparring session","type":"bullet"},{"text":"A single session of 3 × 3-min sparring produced increased corticomotor inhibition, altered motor unit recruitment, and reduced memory performance at one hour, recovering by 24 hours","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Symptom responses appear individual-specific, associated with high impact density and above-average-magnitude impacts — meaning there is no known safe dose","type":"bullet"},{"text":"In professionals, cumulative sparring exposure has been associated with impaired cognitive processing","type":"bullet"},{"text":"Training injuries in amateur boxing, though less frequent than competition injuries, appear more severe","type":"bullet"},{"text":"The conclusion is not “don’t spar.” You cannot learn to fight without fighting, and nothing substitutes for a live opponent with intent. The conclusion is:","type":"text"},{"text":"> Extract the maximum learning per impact. Never take an impact that isn’t buying something no cheaper method could buy.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"9.1 Why this is the most consequential section in the entire system","order":1,"section":"LR-136","source":"LR-136 (The Long Road, Part 6, 9.1 Why this is the most consequential section in the entire system)","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"A boxer advances a stage only when all of these are true:","type":"text"},{"text":"1. Technical competence demonstrated at the current stage across 4+ sessions","type":"text"},{"text":"2. Defensive competence specifically — can maintain guard, avoid or absorb the majority of incoming, and does not panic","type":"text"},{"text":"3. Emotional regulation — does not lose composure when hit; does not escalate intensity beyond the agreement","type":"text"},{"text":"4. Physical capacity — completes the prescribed rounds without technical collapse","type":"text"},{"text":"5. The boxer wants to. A boxer pushed into hard sparring before readiness learns fear, not skill, and the fear is durable","type":"text"},{"text":"Regression is normal and not a failure. After a layoff, an injury, a bad experience, or a concussion, drop back two stages and rebuild. Boxers who return straight to Stage 7 after time out get hurt.","type":"text"}],"drill_refs":[],"heading":"9.3 Progression criteria","order":2,"owner_rules":[{"changed_by":"Jason 2026-11-01 (D-PK71-6)","owner_source":"DOC-027 (Punxsy Master Source Manual v1, Return to Training and Disruption Reentry Source Manual v3, Reentry Assessment Order)","owner_text":["Movement and stance quality.","Cue response and attention quality.","Fatigue sensitivity.","Pressure response under low-to-moderate load.","Readiness for prior live level."],"rule":"After a layoff, injury, bad experience or concussion the return level is set by the owner's reentry assessment in its order (movement and stance, cue response and attention, fatigue sensitivity, pressure response, readiness for the prior live level), reinstalling before progressing; the Long Road line stays as source text."}],"section":"LR-138","source":"LR-138 (The Long Road, Part 6, 9.3 Progression criteria)","storage":"verbatim text on the record (D-PK57)"},{"blocks":[{"text":"9.6.1 Equipment","type":"subheading"},{"header":["Item","Specification"],"rows":[{"Item":"Mouthguard","Specification":"Custom-fitted. Not boil-and-bite. Non-negotiable for a competitive boxer"},{"Item":"Gloves","Specification":"16 oz for sparring; 18 oz for heavier boxers or size mismatches"},{"Item":"Headgear","Specification":"Appropriate to the stage. Evidence indicates head guards plus modern thicker gloves significantly reduced knockouts and head injuries, though facial cuts increase without them"},{"Item":"Hand wraps","Specification":"Correctly applied, every time"},{"Item":"Groin protection","Specification":"Always"},{"Item":"Chest protection","Specification":"Available for female boxers by preference"}],"type":"table"},{"text":"9.6.2 Matching","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Partners matched on weight (ideally within one class, absolute maximum two), experience, and — most importantly — temperament. One partner who cannot control intensity ruins the entire training method for everyone. This is a coaching decision, not a negotiation between boxers.","type":"text"},{"text":"9.6.3 Supervision","type":"subheading"},{"text":"A coach present, watching, and empowered to stop the round. Sparring without supervision is not training; it is unregulated fighting.","type":"text"},{"text":"9.6.4 The pre-round agreement","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Before every session, stated aloud: 1. The intensity level, agreed by both 2. The objective for each boxer 3. The stop signal","type":"text"},{"text":"Any escalation beyond the agreement ends the session. This is a rule, not a suggestion, and enforcing it is the single clearest marker of a well-run gym.","type":"text"},{"text":"9.6.5 Immediate stop criteria","type":"subheading"},{"text":"Stop the round immediately for: - Any concussion symptom — headache, dizziness, fogginess, nausea, light or noise sensitivity, feeling “off,” “not right,” or slowed - Any loss of coordination or balance - Any moment where a boxer stops defending intelligently — this is the clearest observable sign that something is wrong - Visible fatigue degrading defense - Any injury - Any escalation past the agreement","type":"text"},{"text":"9.6.6 The post-sparring routine, every single time","type":"subheading"},{"text":"1. Cool-down, hydration, immediate nutrition","type":"text"},{"text":"2. Symptom screen — a 30-second checklist, taken seriously","type":"text"},{"text":"3. Log: rounds, stage, subjective head-impact score (0–3), technical notes","type":"text"},{"text":"4.
